speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: OIL SEED AND PROTEIN FEED-STATEMENT ON ADEQUACY OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agreed yesterday to make a statement on the oil seed and protein feed situation.
Our assessment is that over-all protein supplies for livestock and poultry will be adequate until the new crop. As a result of action by the United States, our supplies of soybean meal will be less than normal and substitutions will have to be made.
Considerable information has been assembled on supply and export commitments, but more accurate figures will be available respecting export plans when my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), has received actual details on contracts. Such information has been requested from all exporters. The deadline for transmission is midnight tonight, July 5, 1973.
Apart from soybeans and soybean meal, we are optimistic that we will be able to export previously contracted normal supplies to traditional customers.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: OIL SEED AND PROTEIN FEED-STATEMENT ON ADEQUACY OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement is very much appreciated, but somewhat ambiguous. It is very difficult to understand how it will be possible to export protein material according to prior contracts made and at the same time suggest there will be limited supplies, perhaps not enough, of protein from soybean to look after the protein requirements of the livestock industry.
It would be necessary for the government to state it would be prepared to see that proteins of all kinds will remain in Canada in adequate supply to make it possible for the livestock industry to fit it to its normal production rates, particularly in view of the present price of foods.

Meat production costs cannot do anything but adversely affect meat prices in an already expansive market.
The minister did not say anything with regard to the protein sources which come from the fishing industry, such as herring meal and fish meal, but it seems these must have been included in the normal export structure mentioned in the latter part of his statement. It might be necessary under the circumstances for the government to give further consideration to a restriction on commitments of export of protein material in the fish meal area. We sincerely hope that when this inventory is made, the total protein requirement, including the actual requirement from vegetable sources, will be protected for Canadian customers and producers throughout this land in the interest of the consumers of Canada.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: OIL SEED AND PROTEIN FEED-STATEMENT ON ADEQUACY OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments will be brief. The statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is that the supply of protein products in this country will be adequate until the new crop year. I hope that not only the supply of protein in this country will be adequate, but the price the farmer has to pay for those supplies because of the United States embargo will not become sky high. This not only affects the farmers in terms of their own business of producing poultry, livestock and so on, but it affects the consumers because of what they have to pay for these products at the retail level.
I hope the minister can guarantee not only an adequate supply of soybean and protein materials, but that they will be available to the farmer at a decent price so the effect on the consumer will be minimal. I also think the government and the Minister of Agriculture should protest loudly to the United States against the embargo they have placed on the export of soybeans to Canadian mills to the great inconvenience of farmers and consumers.
One other thing is very clear. It is the need in this country for the orderly marketing of all grains, and I cannot let this opportunity pass without suggesting to the government that the time has now come to put all grains under the control of the Wheat Board so that all grains may be subject to orderly marketing. If this had been done earlier, we probably would not find ourselves in a situation such as exists today.
[ Translation]

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: OIL SEED AND PROTEIN FEED-STATEMENT ON ADEQUACY OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we thank the minister for making a statement as he had promised. Still, there is one thing we fail to understand. The minister says the reserves will be adequate until the next crop and, at the same time, that this year's crop will not be as bountiful as he had expected.
I cannot understand that point of view, seeing western Canada has had the reputation in the last few years of being the world's second granary. I fail to understand why the minister did not convince farmers that the production of proteins is profitable, and encourage them to seed more protein grains that might be obtained at a reasonable price, and that the consumers might not have to face another increase in food prices next year.
To my mind, the minister's statement is a prelude to a probable increase of a few cents in the cost of red meats next year.
July 5, 1973

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the prevailing uncertainty concerning oil and gas in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimous-ki (Mr. Allard):
That this House adjourn immediately pursuant to Standing Order 26, first, to consider the possibility of building a pipeline which would bring petroleum products to eastern refineries which are dangerously dependent on imported oil; second, to make adequate studies on the storage of natural gas and oil in the context of a storage policy so as to better serve eastern Canada and make reserves to remedy any shortage stemming from an international crisis with other producer countries; and third, to find new financial facilities at a reasonable rate of interest to assist the financing of this great undertaking and prevent an increase in consumer prices.

speechtext: Let us not confuse crop years and taxation years. We are talking about taxation years. At any time during a crop year, if a farmer delivers grain he has an option. subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext: This clause would amend the personal tax exemptions and rate schedules that take account of increases in prices. The adjusting has been referred to as indexing and is intended to end the erosion of purchasing power resulting from the interaction of inflation with the progressive income tax system.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this of course is one of the key questions in this bill. It brings into effect something that had been laughed at, jibed at and ridiculed by the minister in the past. I do not know whether the minister or his advisers have read the Canadian Tax Journal and some of the articles which appear there.
Mh. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton): We not only read it but we contribute to it.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
The minister says he contributes to it. Perhaps that relates to the part where the editors bring up the odd-ball situation in the tax system which appears from stands or positions taken by the government in some cases before either the Tax Review Board or the Federal Court and all the way to the Supreme Court. We see there some indications of contributions by the federal government through the Department of Justice.
Be that as it may, I think one must say, first of all, that even in 1972 there was an article which appeared at page 327 of the Canadian Tax Journal, by a Mr. George Vuke-lich. It is entitled "The effect of inflation on real tax rates." This article, while it deals in rather sophisticated macroeconomic and mathematical formulas which defy the laymen comes to the conclusion, however, that what inflation has done to the real rates of taxation in this country, particularly any changes in tax rates and reductions in tax rates, is absolutely fantastic.
Therefore, I shall place on record some of the comments of George Vukelich as well as the proposals of the minister at this time. This appears in the May-June, 1973, edition of the Canadian Tax Journal, which I see the minister's adviser has in front of him. It would be interesting if the minister would read what is said about this proposal. It is interesting that the authors say this proposal of the minister is equivalent though not identical to an earlier proposal advanced by the Leader of the Opposition in the May, 1972, budget debate. I think it is well worth putting these observations on the record:
It has traditionally been assumed that an automatic adjustment of tax rates to reflect the effects of price inflation would seriously weaken the macroeconomic stabilizing properties of the tax system, and that such automatic adjustment would consequently increase the price inflation for which it adjusted. Though this assumption might seem ironic in view of the recent ineffectiveness of Canadian macroeconomic policy in combatting inflation, it would (if correct) be a serious argument against the value of implementing the Turner indexing proposal.
The authors examined this from three different points of view. First of all they looked at inflation and the equity considerations underlying tax rates. We look at inflation from the point of view of the governmental sector. This is the point the Leader of the Opposition and others of our party referred to in expounding our theories. As as matter of fact, on two or three occasions in the past in committee, going back five or six years-I do not want to say, "I told

you so"-we actually indicated that the government had a built-in interest in inflation because of the type of tax system we have, the ad valorem way of computing sales tax, customs duties and other taxes levied by the federal government outside of income tax. The government benefits from increases in prices and our steeply progressive- progressive only in the mathematical sense-income tax system which yields it far more money every year due to inflation. In fact, the authors of this article prove without any equivocation that the tax reductions proposed under the 1971 income tax changes, the so-called tax reform-all those lower rates, all the elimination from the tax brackets of 750,000 taxpayers-were eliminated by 1973 as a result of inflation. I quote again:
The effect of inflation on effective real tax rates has been clearly presented in George Vukelich's article in an earlier issue of this Journal. The important effect of inflation on the tax rate schedule is to shrink the real width of tax brackets and to decrease the real value of exemptions; between 1954 and 1970 this had the effect of increasing the effective tax rate on an individual with an unchanged real gross income of $15,000 by approximately one-third. (Statutory changes over the same period caused a slight further increase in effective tax rates.)
Vukelich estimated that by 1974 the tax reduction for this same individual resulting from the tax schedule changes in the 1971 tax reform act would have been eliminated by the effect of inflation. In fact, thanks to the recent acceleration in price inflation, they have already become eliminated in April, 1973. In effect, the reductions in tax rates which partially compensated middle income taxpayers for the reform-induced expansion of the tax base were eliminated by price inflation within 16 months of their becoming effective.
That is the so-called tax reform which, frankly, as a result of inflation was totally wiped out for the broad band of income tax payers in this country. Let us see what the result of inflation is in the governmental sector of the gross national product.
The increases in effective tax rates induced by general price inflation result in an increased share of gross national product being diverted to government. The fact that the GNP elasticity of the personal income tax is substantially greater than unity is well known.
Mr. Chairman it is a most evident fact that an examination of the changes in the GNP share of the tax dollar shows a 329 per cent increase in personal income tax over the period 1961 to 1970 in which the constant dollar gross national product increased by 116 per cent. In other words, for a 116 per cent increase in GNP from 1961 to 1970-that is, in constant dollars-there was a corresponding 329 per cent increase in the yield of personal income taxes, and this all due to inflation. The article continues:
Allowing for . . . changes in rates and assuming the same elasticity of personal taxes with respect to prices as with respect to real per capita income, we can conclude that roughly 40 per cent of the increase in per capita direct personal taxes over the 1964-71 period was due to general price inflation.
What this implies is that government revenues from direct personal taxes would have grown by approximately 13 per cent per year over this period instead of by 18.6 per year, had the rates of all direct personal taxes been indexed for current changes in the consumer price index over this period.
In other words, the proposal if it had been in force would have seen a substantial decrease in the share of personal income taxes paid by private individuals in this country over that period.
July 5, 1973

The indexing proposals advanced by finance minister Turner in his February, 1973, budget call for indexing only the rates and exemptions of the personal income tax, and would have an effect equivalent to perhaps four-fifths of the effect of indexing all direct personal taxes completely. They clearly reduce substantially the growth in tax revenues that is built into the structure of the current tax system.
This was the proposal put forward by the Leader of the Opposition well over a year ago which was ridiculed and scorned by the Minister of Finance from June right through until after the election as being a bankrupt policy for Canada. Yet on the basis that now this is academically approved-Professors Bossons and Wilson give it their full approval-and now that it has been put forth by the minister in his budget of last February, the whole idea, instead of being bankrupt lunacy has become totally acceptable and is now the orthodox policy of this government. This is a clear indication of just how far this government is prepared to be a man for all seasons at all times. In whatever direction the wind may blow, we will find the government lining up. Why? Merely to keep in power.
Although they do not make the statement that one can draw such conclusions from the proposal, I am satisfied that it will be complicated; there is no doubt about it. On the other hand, I am glad that the minister came to his senses and that his colleagues, who perhaps did not understand any of it, went along with him. Now we find the government once more having done a more than 180 degree swing around and accepting a proposal from the opposition. I am glad to support this clause.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the tax deduction clause. The amendment provides for a new deduction from a tax that is otherwise payable. It applies in addition to increased personal exemption. A taxpayer would compute his federal basic tax using new exemptions, but from his basic tax he will then deduct the greater of $100 or 5 per cent of the basic tax. If 5 per cent of the basic tax calculation produces an amount that is more than $500, he will deduct $500; in other words, it is a 5 per cent deduction with a minimum of $100 and a maximum of $500.
Since the provincial tax is computed on the basic tax before making the new $100 or 5 per cent deduction, the provincial tax will not be affected by the new deduction and it will not bring into play any aspects of the fiscal arrangements act. The fact that there is a minimum deduction of $100 results in this measure giving much more than a 5 per cent reduction for over 85 per cent of Canadian taxpayers. A taxpayer's basic tax must be at least $2,000 before the 5 per cent thereof exceeds $100.
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
The income levels at which 5 per cent of the basic tax becomes greater than $100 are as follows: a single person with no dependants earning $11,090; married people with no dependants, $12,491; and married persons with two dependants, $13,091. If the deduction at 5 per cent of the basic tax did not have a ceiling it would produce a large reduction in the tax for those with very high incomes. The income levels at which the $500 ceiling becomes effective are as follows: a single person with no dependants earning $33,786; married people with no dependants, $35,186; and married people with two dependants, $35,786.
In addition to the reductions in tax resulting from increased exemptions and the new $100 or 5 per cent deduction from tax, the tax reform amendments passed in December, 1971, provided new reduced rate schedules in 1973 to 1976 inclusive. These rate schedules remain in the act. A new schedule for 1973 provides that the rate of tax on the first $500 of taxable income shall drop from 17 per cent to 15 per cent. This gives nearly every taxpayer a reduction of at least $10 compared with 1972.
In other words, what we have done here is to introduce a very progressive reduction in tax worth $1,300 million to Canadian taxpayers, putting that back into the pockets of Canadians, and of that $1,300 million in tax cuts $900 million, or 70 per cent, goes to those who are in the $10,000 income bracket or less.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for once I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on the fact that this tax reduction is certainly an improvement; it will of course affect the ordinary, low-income workers. But I would ask the hon. minister whether, in addition to this reduction he has not also considered giving the workers permission-and I stress the word permission-to deduct from their taxes the cost of the tools or special clothing needed for their work, in some cases, in short, to give them the same advantages given to professionals or others.
For example, a construction worker is not allowed to deduct the cost of the tools he needs. Noranda mine workers are not allowed to deduct the cost of the special clothing they need to go down the mines to depths of 5,000 to 7,000 feet, whereas a dentist can deduct the cost of the little white overall he wears, or of his instruments, such as his drill, or an accountant can deduct the cost of a chair, or a desk used for his work. Is the hon. minister therefore considering granting to the working man, to the small wage-earner, as we call him, the same advantages now granted to others? That is the point I am making.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can briefly answer my friend, the hon. leader of the Social Credit Party, that this has already been done.
For example, a $150 deduction is provided for each worker, in respect of tools or clothing. This is already a provision of the Income Tax Act. So I agree in the principle with the hon. member.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
But it is limited. The allowed deduction is only $150, while professionals, dentists, doctors, etc., deduct 100 per cent of their expenditures.
In my business, for instance, when I buy equipment and tools, these expenses are included in my operating costs, while the workman is not entitled to deduct such expenses. Therefore, it seems to me that this $150 deduction should be replaced by the total expenses of the workman, the miner or the construction worker.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this clause is probably the basic part of the changes that are before us today in terms of a real change in direction in the principle of taxation that is based on equity. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, the $100 minimum for every taxpayer is a tax credit. The minister has also imposed a ceiling of $500 in this clause. This is a new and very important step, and I hope it is only the first step toward a tax credit system in our country.
I want to take two or three minutes to urge the House to get away from the system of exemptions and go to a system of tax credits. That system benefits the low and middle income earner much more than a system of tax exemptions. To give three examples of what I mean, hon. members will recall that Bill C-259 which came to this House last year increased the exemption from $1,000 to $1,500 for single taxpayers. That meant a saving for all

Canadians, but the tax saving was greater for those with a higher income. Take a single person earning $2,000 as a gross income: by increasing the exemption from $1,000 to $1,500 the single person is indeed saving $33 a year, but a person earning $4,000 gross income is saving $160 a year. A person earning $25,000 gross income who is single saves $297 a year. This is indeed a much greater saving than for the person earning $2,000 or $3,000. To a person earning $50,000 the $1,500 exemption would mean a saving of $364 annually.
The argument advanced by members of this party is that it would be much more equitable for the low and middle income earner if a new system of tax credits could be devised. Instead of having a $500 increase in exemptions, it would be better to have a $100 or $200 tax credit for everyone paying tax. This would mean a lot more to the low and middle income earner. The clause in the bill before us is a start toward that type of system. I should like to encourage the minister to conduct studies into the transfer to a tax credit system as quickly as possible, because it is a step toward the low income earner reaping the benefit, and in the long term I think the whole economy would benefit.
The hon. member for Edmonton West was concerned about who pays the tax, the upper income level and the corporations, but I suggest that a tax credit system would put more funds into the hands of the low income earner. These funds would be used for food, shelter and clothing and in turn would create jobs, stimulate the economy, provide much greater impetus in general and also put more tax dollars at the other end of the economic scale. I urge the government to continue in this direction. The $100 minimum tax credit is an important principle and one which we certainly commend.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure you will recall that I raised a certain matter yesterday in the hope that the minister might take some initiative in dealing with the problem that I brought to his attention, but judging from the resolution he put before the House earlier today I am afraid he did not.
I am rising at this point to ask the minister if he would be good enough to give an indication of why he resists what to me would obviously be a step in the direction of providing equity in our tax system. While I certainly do not quarrel with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville about this forward step in our tax system, it is but a small step in the right direction. I am completely at a loss to understand why the minister and some of his predecessors have failed to recognize that if we are to have equity of income tax, those who derive income from wages or salaries should have applied to their gross earnings the same principles as are applicable to farmers and to executives of corporations in respect of expenses.
If the approach that I have suggested is not in the minister's view the most appropriate way to deal with this problem, I would certainly welcome some concrete suggestion from him on what approach might be taken to overcome this very long-standing discrimination against workers who go to isolated sites in Canada and while engaged in producing the basic wealth of our economy spend a
July 5, 1973

large part of their working lives away from their homes and families. At the same time, in the course of their employment they take cuts in income because of the rigid application of the income tax rules with regard to deductibility.
Within the last year or so the Prime Minister has made a number of statements urging workers to leave the welfare and unemployment rolls in the cities and go to places where work is available. I tell the minister that at this very time in many areas of the country, including the forest producing areas of my constituency, employers are finding it increasingly difficult to man their operations because of the reluctance of people to engage in difficult and arduous work and, at the same time, incur the kinds of penalties to which they are subject, some of which stem from our income tax laws. Such people are expected to go to areas in which there are not the amenities to which we are accustomed in our urban-oriented society. I am referring to amenities which Canadians take for granted and which ordinarily go with life in this country. Let me mention here the lack of television and radio entertainment, lack of access to libraries for those who are interested, and that sort of thing.
I could mention, as well, the lack of adequate health care facilities in the immediate vicinity of these isolated sites and the dangers that go with that. There is a danger of permanent disability because of the time lapse in obtaining adequate medical care. If one adds to these kinds of things the fact that these people must pay a penalty for the privilege of working, because they must pay for extra board and travel expenses-in many cases expensive air travel if they want to see their wives and families occasionally-one can see the difficulty. This is a situation which I suggest we should explore if we are to restore some balance in our economy and maintain the productive capacity of which we are capable and undoubtedly need in our resource-producing industries. We can do that only if these inequities in our tax system are eliminated. For the life of me, I cannot understand why they are not eliminated. The only excuse I have heard from ministers of finance is that there is difficulty in administration. This matter goes back a good many years. I remind the minister that today there are such things as data processing centres and systems. If that objection was valid 20 years or 15 years ago, I submit it is no longer valid.
Certainly, administration would be no more difficult than administration of the long-standing provisions of the Income Tax Act with regard to the deductibility of medical expenses. If only administrative difficulties stand in the way of the Minister of Finance acting in this area, I suggest he should say to the responsible people in the administration. "This has to be done. You figure out a proper administrative way to do it." I am sure, considering the trained minds that are available to the minister, we could come up with a rational and reasonable system that would not lend itself to abuse but would provide some real equity in the matter I am putting before the minister. I should like him to give me some response other than the sort of suggestions he has made in a genial way across the floor, because this is an important matter not only to the
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
individuals concerned but in the long term to the economy of Canada.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully. We put in the $150 general deduction, we have put in a deduction for moving expenses and we have put in an allowance for child care expenses, as well as an allowance for distant employment site expenses. I will certainly take the hon. member's comments into consideration.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one more point. The matter of expenses for distant and remote sites is applicable only if those costs are paid by the employer. This applies, to my knowledge, fairly generally in the construction industry. I am referring mainly to our resource-production industries where work is carried on at remote sites. Of course, I am also talking about mining and forestry and, in some cases, the fisheries. In most cases those expenses are payable by the individual out of his gross pay cheque. In some cases the rate of board is fixed under union contract. I am talking of the over-all figure. Certainly that applies in the forest products industry of British Columbia.
We have gone beyond the original arrangement which applied only to construction workers and which was brought in by Hon. Donald Fleming in 1957. Having made that provision generally applicable to all workers on remote sites, if the employer pays the shot over and above the wage-and this is the point-the employer is not obliged under the law as it now stands to consider that as part of the earnings of the employee. On the other hand, if the employer pays the whole shot as part of the gross wage directly to the employee, the employee is stuck with his air fare and paying board because they are part of his taxable income. That is a remaining discrimination which applies to one person but not to another doing identical work; and it results from a decision made by the employer, not by the employee. That is the conundrum to which I am drawing the attention of the minister and I should like to see it answered.
I think the most rational way of doing it would be to make a slight change to the Income Tax Act. There would have to be proper administrative safeguards, of course, so that nobody could make a claim out of thin air. Claims would need to be substantiated in the normal way, just as medical expenses over and above the generally allowed deduction need to be substantiated. Expenses could easily be certifiable, in some instances by a supplementary return from the employer. That is what I ask the minister to look at, if he will.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my point here arises out of deductions that must be made by an employer with regard to the Canada Pension Plan. This has created a headache for employers. Employers with a partly rotating work force, or known regular work force have to make deductions with regard to their employees even though the total contributions by employers during the year will far exceed the entitlement of the individual concerned. If the individual concerned has an overpayment he can claim a refund from the Canada Pension Plan. This is done on his income tax return. However, the employer is not entitled to any refund. There is a windfall gain to the Canada Pension Plan of millions of dollars a year.
Situations crop up where an individual is self-employed; for example, doctors and other professionals. As a selfemployed person he has to make the full contribution to the Canada Pension Plan. If he attends university on a very limited, part-time basis, addresses seminars or teaches summer courses, in many instances he receives a nominal stipend. The university authorities are compelled to make a deduction for the Canada Pension Plan. However, as a self-employed person he has already made his total contribution. There is a maximum amount that you pay under the Canada Pension Plan; it is not dependent upon your total earnings but upon earnings up to a certain level.
The individual can claim a refund of the excessive contribution that has been deducted from his stipend and paid by the university, college or whatever body it may be. It may be a professional body. He may receive a stipend for appearing at an annual conference. Under the Canada Pension Plan there is a level to the contribution under those circumstances. However, the so-called employer, whether it is a national association, university or community college has made a contribution to the Canada Pension Plan fund for no reason. There is no way of reclaiming it.
Some members may wonder why I am talking about the Canada Pension Plan under these circumstances. It is because the overpayment of contributions to the Canada Pension Plan are recoverable. In the case of deductions for unemployment insurance, and so on, the minister has authority to make adjustments if there are particular hardships. As a matter of fact, this amendment speaks of particular and undue hardship. This is not an undue hardship upon these associations except for the bookwork, added expense and the dishonesty of it. It is dishonest to take this money from the employer for an employee who is already totally covered and will not have his benefits increased one iota.
The Minister of Finance and his colleagues must bend their attention to the unnecessary gouging of millions of dollars a year from employers which merely go into the Canada Pension Plan. I put it earnestly to the minister that it is not enough to dismiss it by saying it is administratively difficult. That is a lot of poppycock. There is no administrative justification for gouging Canadian employers of millions of dollars a year for an unnecessary pur-
July 5, 1973

pose. In fact, it is totally superfluous to the entitlement of the employee under the Canada Pension Plan.

Mr. Chairman, this proposed amendment is well received by this hon. member. I am sure there are a number of members who have been concerned with taxation on production quotas, and the fact that they are classified as "goodwill" or "nothing". I should like to remind the committee and the minister that the acquisition of a dairy or any type of production quota implies the right to produce, but it also implies an obligation to fulfil that production. I think that is a very important aspect in terms of supplying food to Canadians. As you can see, this is not a one-sided thing at all.
Under Bill C-170 the acquisition of quotas after December 31, 1971, or January 1, 1972, was changed with the result that taxes on gains went up by 2 Vi per cent per year, but was not as onerous as had been contemplated. I felt this was a step forward. Many representatives of farm organizations and a number of members of parliament have been in communication with the minister in an attempt to get the government to recognize the fact that these quotas which were acquired before 1972 should be treated in a manner that was similar. Very often the interpretation of an amendment is different from the expectation of the Minister of Finance. To cite an example I would refer to clause 30 of the Income Tax Act, which refers to the assessment in respect of a part-time farmer. This is interpreted quite differently, in my view, by the national revenue department. We have had a great deal of discussion about this with the Minister of National Revenue.
The only way to acquire a quota is to purchase one or inherit it. Those acquired before that particular date were in a different category. I presume the minister envisaged an evaluation day as has been requested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other farm groups. There are three ways to acquire a production quota; you can inherit one, you can buy one or you can marry one, and sometimes that is not the greatest way. I looked very diligently, with the assistance of my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the parliamentary legal officer, to find a way to amend Bill C-193 with just

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORT ON MANITOBA
speechtext:
On June 14, 1973, a notice of objection in the form of a motion was filed with Mr. Speaker in the following terms:
That, pursuant to section 20 of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act (chapter E-2, R.S.C., 1970), consideration be given by this House to the matter of an objection to the provisions of the report of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the province of Manitoba, laid before this House by Mr. Speaker on May 22, 1973, on the grounds set forth hereafter:
1.	The failure of the commission to recognize the tolerance percentages allowed under the act and the drawing of the boundaries so that rural representation is numerically equal to urban representation as to the numbers of voters in each riding.
2.	The drawing of the boundaries of the electoral districts fail to take note of geographic, trading and social structures, particularly of the rural ridings.

3.	The drawing of the boundaries so that the city of Winnipeg, comprising approximately one-half of the population of Manitoba, is a significant component in nine different constituencies of Manitoba.
4.	And such other objections that the undersigned members may consider applicable in order to carry out the spirit and terms and conditions of the act in question.
Hort. W. G. Dinsdale (Brandon-Souris): Mr. Speaker, the objection to the recommendation of the boundaries commission has been formally made pursuant to section 20 of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. I wish to take this opportunity in speaking to the objection to enlarge on some of the points that were made in the formal objection.
This is the second time that parliament has had the opportunity to deal with boundaries redistribution and adjustments under the terms of the new legislation, the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. I participated in the debate on the first occasion. The objections on that occasion were just as strong as the objections that are being made at present, and I think that the repetition of the objections is an indication that there is something fundamentally wrong with our method of electoral boundaries readjustment.
The act as it was passed back in 1969 was designed to remove redistribution from the realm of partisan politics. Based on the experience of the former and present adjustment, I would say that the act has not only removed the process of distribution from the realm of partisan politics but it has removed the process from the realm of politics absolutely. I say that because there were amendments made to the original act which we suggested, when they were made, would result in the situation that confronts parliament at present. I refer to the amendment which removed representation from the two major political parties of the House of Commons, that is, the government party and representation from the official opposition as members of the commissions in each of the provinces.
The original act as it was presented to parliament included these representatives because it was felt that if you were going to get a redistribution that made sense in terms of the prevailing economic, geographic and sociological circumstances of the riding, it would be necessary to have on the boundaries commissions representatives who had had some exposure to the realities of practical politics. Once the act was amended to remove this input of practical reality it meant that the whole process of redistribution was relegated to those who might have some academic understanding of the political process, and certainly in most instances at least they will be pure from the standpoint of partisan politics, but as has happened in the practical realities of distribution they will fail utterly to even implement the will of parliament as expressed in the act as it was finally passed.
The objections that have been phrased in the formal presentation that has been made by several members from the province of Manitoba deal with three points: first, the failure of the commission to recognize the tolerance allowance under the act. This is a vital part of the whole process of redistribution if we are going to get an equitable balance between the urban community and the rural com-
July 5, 1973

munity. Parliament strongly recommends, and it is so enshrined in the act, that in order to make up for the imbalance in this regard that is inevitable, the redistribution commission should be permitted an upward or downward tolerance of 25 per cent.
With reference to the redistribution in Manitoba, the commission has not only ignored that recommendation but they have aggravated the problem. I refer to my own constituency of Brandon-Souris which is primarily rural and therefore should have some advantage downward in terms of the percentage. Rather than giving that advantage to a rural constituency, the commissioners have erred on the other side of the register and the population figure that they are recommending for this rural constituency is 85,000, some 3 per cent above the quotient of 82,000. You can see that the commission has failed utterly to implement the wishes of parliament as expressed in the legislation that is behind the boundaries redistribution.
Hon. members and constituents were given an opportunity to present their objections to the recommendations in a series of hearings that were held during the month of March. At the hearing in the city of Brandon which took place on March 15 and occupied a whole day, every town and every rural municipality was present. They spent the whole day expressing their objections to the recommendations of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the province of Manitoba. We were hopeful that on the basis of those objections the necessary amendments would be made because it was our sense at the meeting that the commission had been convinced that there had to be further readjustments. However, when the final recommendation came before parliament we discovered that not one iota of change was made. Not only was the wish of parliament thwarted in terms of the tolerance principle, but the vox populi, public opinion, was completely ignored by the commissioners who were obviously working on an academic basis rather than on the basis of practical political reality. I repeat again that it is due to the fundamental flaw in the act where the amendment removed the possibility of practical input.
I do not want to occupy the entire time because there are others who want to speak, but I would underline and emphasize the basic objection to the recommendations as they have come from the hands of the commissioners.

Mr. Speaker, in commenting on this bill I should like to reiterate what has already been stated by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) as I too come from a rural area. Many of the criticisms I will make are peculiar to Manitoba but I think they could be related to most parts of Canada.
Perhaps the aspect of the redrawing of the boundaries that has given much comment has been the lack of change in population that has occurred in Canada particularly in the last decade when rural Manitoba, as part of the rural west, had such a great depopulation. Many factors would indicate that this depopulation will perhaps be coming to an end and that in future population changes would not be so great, so the redrawing of electoral boundaries will not have such an impact.
One of the main arguments and disagreements that I have with the commission has been on its failure to take into account the 25 per cent tolerance that was put in to allow constituencies to vary by that amount. I do not think many members would want the full 25 per cent allowance to be given to all rural communities as opposed to 25 per cent more per city, because this would nearly double city populations over rural populations. There may well have been a greater tolerance reserved in Manitoba, but it can be fairly safely said there was no observation of the 25 per cent tolerance in Manitoba. I believe we have in

Brandon, considered a rural constituency, greater than the norm. In my own constituency it was so slightly under the norm as to be considered almost as if all constituencies have to be considered the same.
I think some weighting has to be given to rural constituencies over and above the actual population count. I suggest that the commission may well have been composed of people who necessarily, in the make-up of commissions, come from the cities of the province. They may well have considered that they were not expected to have observed population tolerance and the 25 per cent was only put in there because there was only an occasional riding where it should be considered, such as Churchill, Manitoba.
In the constituency of Dauphin, an area of 300 miles long by 150 miles wide, with people scattered all over the area, there is only one town of 9,000 people, the balance living in hamlets, villages and isolated farms. There is a reasonably good road in the area and the terrain is flat and one can move around fairly easily by automobile, but the enormous distances covered to service the riding should be taken into consideration.
Every member is deluged with service to his constituents on old age pension and unemployment insurance problems and other non-political problems that only he can attend to; but the city dweller has a greater chance of attending to these things himself than the rural dweller. This is very natural because government offices must necessarily be located in the large cities. If a citizen of Winnipeg has a problem with income tax, he can walk downtown to the income tax office and, hopefully, get an opinion, whereas if he lived a couple of hundred miles out this could not be done. Similarly with unemployment insurance and almost all the social services where the officials are concentrated in the city. I believe that the commission in Manitoba has assumed that rural population will continue, and have drawn the boundaries on the basis of what the population will likely be some time in the future; but this is not necessarily so. Perhaps the natural increase will not be so great, and indeed I would hope that in the next decade it would level out.
With this in mind I should like to protest the drawing of the boundaries as presently stated in Manitoba. I should also like to suggest that the commission did not take into account in the rural areas the normal flow of commerce and population movement. In Manitoba we have a general east-west movement of commerce. This is because Winnipeg is situated at the southeastern corner and the settlement of agricultural areas is spread over the west and northwest, so there has been a general movement in this direction. I do not think that the commission has adequately taken into account the natural boundaries,, the flow of commerce and the highway system in drawing their maps.
I should also like to take issue with the fact that the province of Manitoba, with 12 seats, will only have three outside a significant portion of the city of Winnipeg. These would be Brandon-Souris, Dauphin and Churchill, and of these only Dauphin would be a strictly rural constituency representing people who almost wholly make their income from agriculture. Although Winnipeg has half the population of Manitoba, under boundaries as they are drawn there would be a significant Winnipeg population in nine

of the 12 constituencies. I suggest this is not good. Wherever possible, rural and city seats should be completely separated.
In Manitoba, according to the demographic drawing of the boundaries, it is proposed that one seat would be half city and half rural. I believe this should be confined to one riding only. I believe such considerations would be very useful to follow in any redrawing of boundaries. I hope the observations of the present commission will be taken into consideration by future commissions and, when boundaries are redrawn that these considerations will be taken into account. This point should also be considered right across this country. I believe that the lumping together of agricultural and city constituencies, particularly where large cities are involved, is not good and should be avoided wherever possible.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REMOVAL OF LIMITATIONS TO ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN CATEGORIES OF PERSONS IN FEDERAL SERVICE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House the government should consider the advisability of removing all limitations and restrictions whatsoever on the entitlement and payment of pensions, superannuation or retirement allowances of whatever kind to retired members of the Canadian defence forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, senators and members of parliament when any such person so entitled enters into the service of the government of Canada, whether by way of the Public Service Commission or by appointment by the federal authority to any commission, board, or other body or to the judiciary of Canada or in any other manner.
He said: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow's order paper will look different. My motion has been standing at the head of the list for some months and, because its principle was so important, it was being considered in high places. There were discussions regarding its acceptability and I hope that some progress has been made in this connection.
My motion purports to ask the government to consider the advisability of taking certain action with regard to the restrictions now imposed on members of the Canadian Armed Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Members of Parliament and Senators who, having completed their period of service under the Crown in one capacity, would by entering the public service of Canada or by being appointed by the federal government to a board, commission, the bench, or any other type of employment under federal jurisdiction, lose certain pension entitlement by reason of the very outdated application of an old principle that somebody dredged up from I do not know where. That principle suggests that one cannot take two benefits simultaneously from the Crown.
At one stage members of the armed forces on retirement could not enter into the service of the government of Canada without abating their superannuation entirely until their retirement from the public service. It is the same with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Members of Parliament have never suffered from any such abatement.
Let me show how hollow is the application of the principle which says that this matter shall be applied rigidly and that it is sacrosanct. For years now there has been in the armed forces and also in the RCMP the rank of chief warrant officer. It used to be warrant officer class one. Any pension or superannuation payable to a person occupying any rank up to that rank was eliminated, was carved out; therefore it was only commissioned officers in the armed services who were caught by the disability, to the extent that their superannuation allowances exceeded those paid to a chief warrant officer.
This matter involved many highly trained men. The country, for instance, spent a great deal of time training many senior staff officers. This training was thrown away for ten years at least, in the majority of cases. We did not utilize the abilities of these men. There was no way that
Pensions
they were going to take a job with the government of Canada and have their pensions abated because of a formula which said that the salary they would take with their new employment must not exceed the allowances to which they were entitled on retirement. This provision imposed a very grave penalty on many people if they took such employment.
On the other hand, in cases where the Crown was to benefit the principle was sacrificed. It was cut in two for expediency's sake. Strangely enough, if any member of the armed services or RCMP went to work for a provincial government, for the Crown in the name of the province, such restriction did not apply at all. The provinces have been the gainers thereby, because those men who went to work for the provincial governments have been men of ability who have greatly contributed to the efficacy of the public service of the provinces. I am not complaining about that; my complaint is that these men could easily have been available, in most instances, to the public service of Canada.
Because such men have taken the combined benefits, some people have said, "Oh, but they are getting far too much money". We should look at the effects of income tax, which is a great reducer to a common base. Secondly, I find -t absolutely repugnant to think that a man or a woman who has been in the service of Canada in the armed forces, in the RCMP or as a member of the House, should be disentitled to a pension on taking certain other employment. If that individual had worked for a number of years in private industry or been self-employed and had paid into a retirement pension plan, and had then entered the service of the government of Canada, he would have been entitled to bring that pension along with him. That person has contributed to a private plan. The member of the armed services contributes to superannuation; it is part of his pay. The same goes for the RCMP, as well as for the Member of Parliament.
To me, the Member of Parliament who is doing his job, who has to give up his business, give up his profession, or see his business disappear, and is paying into the pension plan, is building up his pension here in the same way as are the officers of the House and in the same way as are other personnel of the House of Commons. That is the way we build up our retirement income. This represents savings. Yet some outdated and outlandish interpretation of the law makes Members of Parliament and Senators flogging horses, or flogging boys. This is too much.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has given this place his lifetime. I apologize for singling him out, but he happens to be here. I could also mention the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale) who has been a member of this House since 1951. He has given the greatest part of his productive years to the service of this country as a Member of Parliament. Both of these are very hard working men and they have a pension entitlement. However, if for some reason or another either of them were to retire from this House-

speechtext:
No, but it would add to his laurels. For him, with his accumulated knowledge, to sit on some board or commission would be of immense value. However, as long as he is in that employment his superannuation entitlement would be in abeyance. If he had come from private industry or anywhere else, he would carry his pension entitlement with him. However, as a Member of Parliament he is not entitled to that. That is utter nonsense.
It must seem strange that we speak about this question in this milieu of ours, but I want to eliminate all that. If a lawyer served as a Member of Parliament for 15 or 20 years, he would be entitled to a pension. If he is appointed to the Bench, whether it is the county court or superior court of a province, there is no way he can draw upon his accumulation of pension entitlement. At the present time, it is payable to his estate. Up until two years ago, it was totally forfeited if one went to the Bench. How ridiculous!
A lawyer who gives up his practice, which is his capital, to serve as a Member of Parliament accumulates a modest pension entitlement. It is certainly very modest compared to the upper levels of the public service and very modest compared to the upper levels in business and industry. In any event, he builds up a modest pension entitlement.
Most lawyers are prudent men. Most judges will say they require some additional revenue to properly maintain their standard of living as a judge. Many judges have told me that if they had not built up capital to give them additional revenue, they could not have accepted the job. However, a Member of Parliament is precluded from doing that unless he has some other source of outside revenue. He pays 714 per cent of his salary into a pension plan. This is a higher contribution than in any other walk of life in Canada. I have read newspaper articles which state this is the most generous pension plan in Canada. Nonsense. It is only that people are totally ignorant of what this pension plan means. They only look at the front end load.
It is true that after six years a young Member of Parliament becomes entitled to a pension. That is one of the features I would like to see reviewed. However, it is not for me to say that such and such a member who is much younger than I should not be entitled to a pension.
When I first came here, the maximum pension was $3,000 a year after 17 years of service. Upon reaching the age of 70, the old age pension was deducted from that. That is how far they carried the principle that you could not receive two benefits from the Crown. That is how ridiculous it was. Now there is this continuing drive.
I hope members will agree this matter should be further aired, and that the subject matter of this motion should be referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. It should also be considered by Treasury Board. We should decide once and for all to do away with this restriction.

I am sure there is no venality or nepotism in the government appointing a Member of Parliament to a commission. There are a lot of such bodies and these men earn their pension. However for some damn fool reason they are not entitled to recovery until they retire from that appointment. In the case of a judge, the contributions will go to his estate.
My last point is whether the pension scheme is generous. Has anyone seen what happens after 15 years' service? The benefit from the contributions goes down dramatically. In certain instances there is a front end load, but not for the average Member of Parliament. For those who have had the benefit of being returned by their constituents for more than 15 years, the whole thing becomes farcical. There is no way you can keep up your contributions to the level to which you are entitled on the basis of the service that has been rendered. There is also the IVi per cent impost which, incidentally, only this year exceeds the allowance under the Income Tax Act. Therefore, a goodly portion of the contributions are doubly taxed, both when they go in and when they come out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had firmly intended to sit this one out, but the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) had occasion in a very kind way to make a reference to me as well as to my good friend and fellow Manitoban, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). Therefore, I should like to say a few words.
I wish to make it clear that in my view the hon. member is doing a service by raising the question of the position, when they are retired and on pension, of former members of the Canadian Armed Forces and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There may be other categories, but those are two categories of public servants where by law they have to retire early. The hon. member is quite right in pointing out that many of these persons have gained considerable expertise and at the time of retirement they could render invaluable service. There is no reason they should be denied the opportunity to render that service to the federal government. They are free to do so in the case of provincial governments, private industry, and so on, so it does not seem sensible they should be denied the right to render further service to the federal government.
Nevertheless, at the risk of inviting some of the epithets the hon. member has been throwing out, I must say to him that I wish he had not included in this motion the reference to Members of Parliament and Senators. I insist that our position is different. There is no point in talking of the pension as it was when the hon. member came here, or as it was not when I first came here. The fact is that it is now, for those who stay around a few years, a generous pension. If a member has been here for six years, no matter what his age, he receives a pension of $3,780 a year for life, subject to a 2 per cent annual escalation. If he stays here for ten years, his pension starts at $6,300 a year for life no matter at what age he begins to draw it. If he enjoys the place so much that he stays around for 25 years or more-and this is an enjoyable place if you stay here that long-his pension will be $13,500 for life subject to a 2 per cent annual escalation provision. Then again, whereas
July 5, 1973

most Canadians find the Canada Pension Plan incorporated with their other pension plans, ours is stacked.
As to Senators, they do not retire until the age of 75. Their pension arrangements, if they have been Senators only, are not quite as good as ours. But if they have been members of this House translated to the other place, their pensions are the equal of ours. I believe there is a difference between those of us who have served in this place of our own free will, with a little public support, and those who become employees of the state, as are members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP.
I have to say with all kindliness to the hon. member, since he tells us that ideas such as mine are foolish, farcical, and so on, that it would not be a wise move for us to change the rules and make it possible for Members of Parliament, having got pensions, to take up a federal government job and get paid twice. We complain, and hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party complain, about the numbers of defeated Liberals who get themselves on the government payroll. Many of them were not around long enough to get a pension, and I suppose the reason they got these jobs is because they had not qualified for a pension. But if it were possible to place on the payroll defeated Liberals who were already drawing pensions, I believe my hon. friend's friends would complain about it even more than they do at present.

I think the hon. member is not right in a technical sense when he says there is some general rule against anyone getting two benefits from the Crown. There are members of this House who draw the family allowance in addition to their indemnity as MPs. I believe there is one member who draws income from three sources under the Crown-
Pensions
his indemnity, his old age pension and the family allowance. There are others who draw war disability pensions and their indemnities, and properly so. These things stand on their own feet. There is no blanket rule. We have the right under law to decide what should be permitted.
Pension schemes are worked out on an actuarial basis. One of the reasons our plan is so generous is because it was assumed from an actuarial point of view that certain things would happen. An attempt to change the provisions of the plan could easily destroy its actuarial basis. I am sorry the hon. member should have made it necessary for me to rise to my feet and divorce myself from the suggestion he made about Members of Parliament, but I must do so, without question. As for Senators, at the age of 75, when they retire-and, as hon. members know, if I had my way I would retire all of them immediately-

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy-Council) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES READJUSTMENT ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-208, to suspend the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, be read the

second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill which is now before the House will have the effect of suspending the provisions of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. The first issue with which the bill deals is the current redistribution. In the past number of weeks we have had the reports of the provincial boundaries commissions as provided for under the present law. It is plain that if the redistribution process currently underway were allowed to proceed it would probably result in a situation where it may be physically impossible to have an election between late this fall and the fall of 1974. That is the first point I want to make. The second is that there are pretty strong indications, particularly from the objections which have been filed in the House of Commons to the reports of the redistribution commissions, that there is considerable dissatisfaction with the results of the present system under which we operate.
This bill, if it carries and is made law, would make it possible for the House of'Commons to consider changes that might bring about a more satisfactory system of redistribution. The first problem, namely the difficulty of impossibility of having an election during a period as long as one year, arises because of the time schedule which is formally established under the present Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. Under the time schedule in the present law the new electoral boundaries resulting from the redistribution currently under way would probably be proclaimed in November or December of this year. If, in the normal course, the objections that have already been filed were debated in the House of Commons and returned for reconsideration to the provincial commissions which would consider them, then returned by the provincial commissions to the Representation Commissioner he would have ready for proclamation this fall the new representation system or the new boundaries affecting the electoral districts in Canada.
Once the proclamation establishing these boundaries was made, any election following that would have to be held on the basis of the new boundaries. However, it is estimated by the Chief Electoral Officer that it would probably take a minimum of one year from the time the new boundaries are proclaimed to prepare for a new election. That arises from the fact that new returning officers would have to be appointed for each of the new electoral districts. Once the returning officers had been selected, they would have to undergo training in order to allow them to carry out their functions. Once all the returning officers were selected and trained, they in turn would have to carry out, in a sense, a mini redistribution in each of the new electoral districts establishing the boundaries of new polling divisions. So much for the administrative side.
On the political side it is probable that the political parties in the country having to fight that election would require considerable time to organize themselves and cope with the problem of running candidates in basically new electoral districts.
July 5, 1973

Consequently, in order to prevent a situation where it would be virtually impossible to have an election for a period of one year, this bill provides that the present electoral boundaries shall remain in force for a period of one year after the new electoral boundaries are proclaimed, whether these new boundaries come about as a result of the present method of redistribution, or any other new method or new system on which parliament might decide. If the House were totally satisfied with the results of the present system and with the new boundaries of each of the new proposed constituencies, it would still require a considerable period of time in order to prepare for a new election and, as I have stated, that period of time would probably extend for at least one year. I cannot foresee that members of parliament or members of the public would accept with any equanimity the possibility that an election could not be held in this country, say, from the fall of 1973 to the fall of 1974. So that is one aspect of the problem.
The second aspect concerns dissatisfaction with the electoral boundaries arising out of the current redistribution process. It would seem that the problem is really the current system of redistribution, or the number of seats allocated to each province. The electoral boundaries being proposed have been arrived at in compliance with the rules and procedures laid down in the present law. None the less, I realize, as do other hon. members, that there is substantial dissatisfaction with the results, as evidenced by speeches in the House by various members and by the number and fundamental nature of the objections to the proposals of the provincial electoral boundaries commissions. As hon. members know, substantial objections have been tabled to the representation commission reports for six provinces to date, and the time period for the tabling of objections for three other provinces has yet to expire, in which case further objections might be expected. Only the report from Prince Edward Island has not had objections registered.
Consequently, with the passage of this act to suspend the current redistribution process it would be possible for parliament to consider how to deal with developing a more appropriate method for redistribution, and the government will be making proposals to the House in this regard, probably in the resumed session. We realize that it is important for members of the House, probably through a parliamentary committee, to consider whether it is possible to bring about a more satisfactory system, whether it be by increasing slightly or substantially the number of members of the House of Commons or some other method that may be developed within the committee. In any event, parliament will have an opportunity to consider whether a more satisfactory system could be developed, and that cannot be done overnight; it will take a lot of thought and consideration by members of all parties.
In order to give adequate time for consideration of a new system of redistribution, this bill will continue the suspension of the necessary sections of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act until January 1, 1975. It is hoped and expected that within that period it will be possible for members of the House to agree on a new system of redistribution that would replace the present system. But to guard against the possibility that at the end of that period parliament has failed to act and to bring
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension about a new system of redistribution, and to avoid the feeling that there may be inherent in this bill a desire to avoid redistribution altogether or to avoid the redrawing of boundaries, there is a provision in the bill that at the end of that period, if results have not been achieved, the present system will be reactivated. We stop the clock, as it were, at the present time and it is not allowed to tick for a period of 18 months. If in that time some alternative system has not been developed, the bill provides for the clock to start ticking again and the whole process currently under way will be reactivated, subject to certain modifications contained in this bill designed to minimize the effect of the suspension.
In keeping with that description of the problem the provisions of the bill can be quite simply divided into three parts: those which deal with the suspension of the existing redistribution process; those which provide for the reinstatement of the process if parliament does not take any action within 18 months; and finally a provision which ensures that there will not be a hiatus during which it would be difficult or impossible to hold an election following the proclamation of a new system or the proclamation of new boundaries affecting all the constituencies of Canada.
Along with the suspension provision of the bill or the suspension of the ongoing process, provision has been made to discharge the existing provincial representation commissions. If the bill becomes law, the present provincial representation commissions which have been sending their reports to the House of Commons would cease working at this stage and would be discharged for the present time.
As I have explained, should no new approach to redistribution be achieved or formulated within 18 months, the existing redistribution process would be reinstated along with the establishment of new representation commissions which would pick up the reports prepared by the existing provincial representation commissions. From the reports that have already been presented and the parliamentary objections that have been tabled, the reconstituted commissions would familiarize themselves with the situation, and then they would hold public hearings. On the basis of these hearings, the reports of the current representation commission and parliamentary objections thereto, the reconstituted commissions would then prepare a report which would be submitted to parliament and would be treated in precisely the same manner as if these reports of the reconstituted commissions were the initial reports of the provincial representation commissions.
Provision is therefore made for parliamentary objections to the reports of the reformed commissions and the debate of the reports and the objections which follow these reports would be returned to the reformed or reconstituted commissions for revision as these commissions believed appropriate. On the basis of the revisions prepared by the reconstituted commissions, the representation commissioner would prepare a redistribution order which, on proclamation, would establish the distribution which would take effect immediately following any dissolution of the House of Commons occurring at least one year after the proclamation order. This one year provision
5344

July 5, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension would avoid the hiatus or interregnum which exists in the current redistribution act.
The framework of the bill is quite simple, if I may summarize it again for hon. members. The first effect the bill would have is to avoid the situation that for a period of one year an election could not be held, as is currently the case; and an 18 month period would be made available to the House of Commons to develop a new system of redistribution. The object of the exercise is that we find in that period of time a more satisfactory system of redistribution. If we fail, then we have to go back to the system we have now. We would have to gear up the process and bring it to the same conclusion that it would have-were it left to continue without any interruption. In the normal course the representation commissioner would issue his proclamation this fall and the next election would be carried out on the basis of the proclamation order. We avoid that for at least 18 months in the hope that we get a better system. If we do not achieve a better system we go back and live with the present system that so many of us find unsatisfactory.
That is the objective of the bill, Mr. Speaker. It is quite simple. Hon. members have probably been informed about it through my colleagues, the house leaders of the other parties. I hope it will be possible to deal with it fairly quickly and have further consideration of any technical considerations or details in the standing committee.
