speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in general I would support this bill and I think it will find guarded favour with many of our group. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction with the way in which the new electoral boundaries have been drawn and a general feeling among many that changes should be made.
It was interesting to note during committee hearings, when I heard the problems of the Chief Electoral Officer, that when the present electoral map was redrawn in effect it could not be brought into force in a practical way for a year. That certainly showed that something had to be done. Whatever the manner the new boundaries are arrived at, whether the present manner or one which this House will devise, this one year period will give the Chief Electoral Officer an opportunity to carry out his duties in a reasonable way. It will also give political parties and candidates a chance to prepare and to make plans on the basis of a reasonable electoral map.
It is interesting that this was not noticed when the present electoral law was drawn up back in the 1960s, and it just goes to show that the best laid plans are not foolproof.
*
Much of the dissatisfaction with the present drawing of the map has no doubt come about because of the very rapid change in population growth, which has shown that the Canadian population is growing at a much faster rate than is the case in many other countries. The population of Canada has increased from something like 18 million in 1961 to almost 22 million in 1971. As well as that, there has been a great shift from rural to urban areas and the various provinces have not grown at the same rate, sometimes due to their attractiveness in climate or development in the economic sense. My own province of Manitoba and the neighbouring province of Saskatchewan have

shown a steady decline in their elected members although they have not lost any population, losing one member each in the present electoral process. There is considerable evidence that this trend could continue.
In the maritime provinces Prince Edward Island is down to their four members, and protected by the number of Senators. In New Brunswick a like situation prevails, with ten members protected by the Senate representation. Newfoundland is at its minimum and Nova Scotia is one above. Manitoba and Saskatchewan could drop down to six members in relation to the number of Senators they have. The province of Quebec will lose two members while Ontario and British Columbia will gain three.
The demand that there should be some means of prorating other than with the number of Senators has been extensively canvassed. It is hoped that whatever method is used to seek out and clarify the situation, representation of provinces will be just and equitable. It will have to take in representation by population as well, I believe, as other factors.
Not everyone will feel that redistribution should be delayed for a second look, especially those provinces that have been growing rapidly. Numerous city ridings have shown a very large increase in their populations in a short time. Some such ridings have doubled their population since the last redistribution. However, this is a feature of rapid population growth and shift in our country, and there are bound to be considerable inequities at any given time in any situation that develops.
The suggestion of a boundary commission appeared to become non-political and, as such, seemed to be an excellent idea. But the idea of commissions composed of those in high and honoured positions does not seem to take into account all those factors that go to make up our population mosaic. The people in charge now largely seem concerned with feeding the appropriate population figures into the computer and drawing maps accordingly.
In my province, Manitoba, the commission seems to have ignored entirely the tolerance of 25 per cent allowed for under the act as between constituencies. This tolerance was to give weight to distance, which was a factor, so that generally allowance could be made to have rural constituencies somewhat smaller than the norm, while city constituencies could be a bit bigger.
While representation by population seems an equitable goal at which to arrive, there is no doubt that constituents living in cities have better access to government offices and officials than do rural constituents, who must necessarily have less service than city constituents. Consequently, the distance factor makes such constituents more dependent on their member of parliament.
The commission also seemed to be extremely insensitive to communities of interest, to the flow of people in natural trading and transportation areas, and seemed to disregard natural boundaries. In my province, Manitoba, it has been contrived that nine out of the 12 ridings will have a significant Winnipeg component, although Winnipeg makes up only about one-half of the total population. There is a general fear on the part of rural constituencies that they will become completely dominated by the city
July 5, 1973

segments, of which they are part. Similarly, perhaps, city constituencies of a largely rural riding area would harbour the same fear.
It seems to me that, wherever possible, the city and rural ridings should be separated, and in matters such as these commissions have not been particularly sensitive to existing needs. I submit that further guidelines must be given to the commission to enable them to draw up more workable constituency maps. I believe that, although the commissions should not be political, they ought to have political input. Having discussed this with hon. members in committees, I believe better guidelines should be drawn.
There has also been a feeling that the number of members of the House should be enlarged. There has been no great change for about 30 years. Thirty years ago our population was a great deal smaller than now. There seems to be a very good case for examining this aspect and seeing whether or not an enlargement of the number of members of the House is desirable. If the number of members in the House remains at the present level, it will mean that in many rural constituencies the area to be covered will be so vast that the member will be known largely by hearsay during his four year term of office. This is particularly true where coverage by radio and television is sparse. Some enlargement of the House might prevent the loss of seats by those provinces falling behind in population growth, without detracting from the proportional increase of those provinces enjoying rapid population growth.
We must also be aware of this: although certain provinces are growing rapidly now, conditions can and almost certainly will change, and the slow growth provinces could well experience a relatively rapid increase in population. This of course, depends on the imponderables of the future.
This bill will receive mixed reaction on the part of many members. However, I wish to give it my qualified support, as I feel that it is time to have an assessment of the number of members, of the representations of the provinces and also, and very importantly, of the question whether or not the functioning of the commission can be improved on. I recognize that not everyone will totally support this view, but I hope that some compromise can be agreed to.
I do not say that we must arrive at a formula that will be satisfactorily forever and anon. No matter what we decide in this House, there will be changes made in the future in methods of redistribution. We must act on the basis of the present situation, because we cannot hope to arrive at a solution that will satisfy members of parliament who will sit here several decades from now. We must look at what is practical now and make provision for the parliaments that will sit in the next decade or so. That is how we should arrange for the redistribution process to be carried on.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing tonight with a bill which is of interest and concern to every member of the House. As a result, there are bound to be differences of opinion, and
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension may I say at the outset that within my party there are different views on some aspects of this bill.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) made reference to what he identifies as a feeling that the system of redistribution has been unsatisfactory. I should like to qualify that. If by the system hon. members are referring to redistribution being done by outside, independent commissions rather than committees of this House, an experience some of us remember vividly, then I say the present system is much better than the former operation. Also, in so far as the present system provides guidelines that aim at representation by population, the present system is much better than the former "non-system" under which there were no guidelines at all. Nevertheless, the workings of the system have produced a number of situations that are bound to be unsatisfactory, and I think it can be said that the purpose of the government in introducing this bill is that of trying to cope with one of these conditions right now, and to provide us with an opportunity to cope with the other one.
I think it is agreed generally, certainly it is in my party-and agreement has already been expressed by the President of the Privy Council and by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie)-that we must correct that oversight that even the best brains in this House did not detect when we passed the present act in the early 1960s. I am referring to the set up under the act which would make it possible for a strange situation to develop, namely, for the Representation Commissioner to proclaim the new boundaries and then for parliament to defeat the government and force an election at a time when an election could not be held because certain technical arrangements had not been met. It seems strange that those who were involved in that debate-mind you, that took place in a majority rather than a minority situation-missed that point.
Therefore, I am sure there will be agreement in all parts of the House that this fundamental change in the law which is proposed by this bill is one that we have to make. We support the proposal that there should be an arrangement for a proclamation leaving a space of time so that, when new boundaries following any redistribution come into effect, it will at that time be possible, if for any reason it becomes necessary, to hold a general election.
It is unthinkable under our parliamentary system that there should ever be a time when'an election cannot be held for technical reasons. So we are glad that the point has been detected, even though it took a minority government situation to bring it to light. We are glad it is to be corrected by this bill.
However, there is another situation that has developed which, in my view at any rate, parliament ought to try to correct. I refer, as did the hon. member for Dauphin and the President of the Privy Council, to the unfair situations that can develop among the various provinces.
If our law was one that went for absolute representation by population with no province being granted any kind of protection, one might push the purist argument and say that it should be carried all the way through. However, we have a situation in which a province like Prince Edward Island, with a population equal to that of one constituency
5346

July 5, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension in some cases, has four seats guaranteed to it. We also have similar guarantees for the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. Yet even among those provinces, there is an unfairness in this system.
New Brunswick and Nova Scotia both have a guarantee that their membership will not fall below 10 because each of them has 10 members in the other place. However, in the case of Newfoundland where there are only six members in the other place. The floor for that province is six members unless, of course, it can get a population above that of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Therefore, there is a gross unfairness even among the Atlantic provinces in the way in which the senatorial floor works.
When we come to my part of the country, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, we find we have been losing seats rather heavily despite the fact our actual population has not declined. For example, when I first came to this House we had 17 members from Manitoba and 21 from Saskatchewan. Now we have 13 each. Under the proposed map, we will drop to 12 each.
I correct my friend from Dauphin. He said that in our case the floor was six. He just read that far into the constitution where it says the number of members a province has in the Senate provides the floor; but there is another provision which provides that once a province has more population than another province with 10 members, it shall not have fewer than that number. In Manitoba and Saskatchewan, each with a population greater than the province of New Brunswick, our membership cannot fall below 10, which is the floor for New Brunswick. But we could fall to 10. Indeed, we could get to the point where we have twice as much population in Manitoba or Saskatchewan as they have in New Brunswick and yet find ourselves with the same number of members.
The arbitrary floors that exist were all right in principle when they were first brought in to protect the then maritime provinces, but the way things have worked out there is now a situation of unfairness as among the smaller provinces. I use the word "smaller" in relation to population.
It seems to some of us that this is a problem that has to be solved. Maybe a way to solve it would be to abolish the principle of a senatorial floor-as far as I am concerned, we could abolish the Senate at the same time-and substitute for it some arbitrary floors picked in a scientific fashion. We could, for example, decide that in the case of Manitoba and Saskatchewan we have gone as low as we should go and should not go any lower, without detracting from the right of Ontario and British Columbia to have the larger number of members to which their population entitles them.
We could develop a system in which we provide for each province a certain number of members, two, three, or four, just because they are provinces. On top of that we could give each province a number of members in proportion to their population. Alternatively, we could decide on quotients that vary. The first 500,000 or one million could represent so many members and after that it would take more population to get additional seats.
The point I am making is there are various ways in which something could be done to resolve this riddle or

unfortunate situation in which provinces like Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia suffer in relation to the other smaller provinces, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. It is not at all inconsistent with the belief in representation by population to press the case that provinces in this country have rights, and that includes the smaller provinces as well as the larger ones.
I have tried to suggest in very vague terms three or four ways in which this problem could be solved so that we would protect the rights of provinces like Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. However, I want to make the point immediately that we cannot solve this tonight. We cannot solve it in this month of July. We are going to need some time. However, as one who is in favour of this bill, I feel it has the advantage that it does give us time to cope with this problem.
If we do not pass this bill and let the present process continue, we will compound the unfairness to provinces like Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. It will somehow settle the issue and it will not come up again for eight or 10 years.
I have every sympathy with those, some of them in my own party, from a province like British Columbia where, under the new map, they will stand to gain seats and perhaps receive a better drawing of the boundaries. I have sympathy with their feeling that it is unfair to them to bring this process to a stop and not let them get what is their right because of their larger population.
I reply to that by saying most people will agree that the next election is likely to be fought on the old boundaries anyway. After all, the next election is not likely to be three or four years from now; it is likely to be in a much shorter time. I feel it would make sense to establish some certainty, not just so that the next election is fought on the old boundaries by default, but rather to establish the certainty suggested in this bill and then do what this bill provides-grapple with this problem of a formula that would be fair to all the provinces.
I say in all frankness that if all this bill proposed was to have the next election on the old boundaries and for nothing to be done about the basic problem, it would be somthing less than honest to support it. The only basis on which one can support this bill is, as the President of the Privy Council said, by being determined to cope with this problem of the ratio of seats among the provinces and to do so this year.
The most important thing the President of the Privy Council said in support of this bill tonight is that the government hopes to propose a solution to this problem in the resumed session. I took it from that he means to propose something when the House resumes in the fall after the summer adjournment, if indeed we have a summer adjournment. That is the main basis on which to appeal to members, especially those in provinces like Ontario and British Columbia where they defer the chance of getting more members, to support this bill.
I want to see them get their additional members, but in all frankness I do not see how they can expect to get them in the next election. I want to be sure they get them in the election after the next. I think they are fair minded people, and they will agree it is not right to continue the
July 5, 1973

unfairness, and indeed compound it against provinces like Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. On that basis I intend to support this measure and a number of my colleagues will do the same.
Some of my hon. friends may wish to press the point that we should not deny Ontario and British Columbia the right to an increased number of members. This is a point of view that I respect, but since I do not see this is as a possibility for the next election, I believe it makes sense to establish some certainty and to give parliament a reasonable amount of time to cope with the basic problem of devising a formula which is fair to the various provinces. It does not make sense or justice to apply cold-hearted arithmetic and give Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia the number to which they are entitled by their populations, to protect provinces like Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and then to leave other provinces such as Newfoundland and Manitoba in between so that they do not have a fair ratio of members.
I urge the House to support this bill but I hope that what the minister said in his opening remarks can be taken as a firm commitment, namely that when we are here this fall a measure will be placed before the House and sent to committee to find an appropriate formula whereby the provinces which are between the protected ones and the larger ones will get their proper number of seats in this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to state my opinion and that of the members of our party on the proposed reforms.
The suggested electoral reforms may be essential, but I do not see for what reason. If the decision is taken to defer those reforms till next year, I think that it would be advisable to do so. I feel that they should be deferred, because they are more or less satisfactory; while they have many advantages for some urban constituencies, they have many drawbacks in rural ridings.
We are wondering, Mr. Speaker, why it is necessary to subdivide the constituencies once again since that was done not so long ago. I know that there have been some changes in the population, but that motive should not be put forward to maintain that it is necessary to subdivide the constituencies every four or five years to upset completely the members' field of action as well as the economic activities of every province.
Faced with these divisions of ridings, the members are quite confused and the voters in some ridings find themselves at a complete loss because by changing them in the way that is desired nowadays, some of them find that they are completely new regions and agglomerations, in which the people are not used to living, talking, meeting or doing business with each other. Moreover, the geographical location does not make it possible for the people to see each other often, which creates problems.
I do not know who has been pushing this idea of dividing ridings. I do not know whether someone wants to increase the value of urban ridings, so as to reduce that of the rural ridings, but there is certainly something under -
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension hand going on, and I will say to the minister that the needs of rural ridings are by no means the same as those of urban constituencies.
I will also say to the minister that the member for a rural riding probably has 50 times more work than the member for an urban riding, because in rural areas we have the problem of agriculture, which doesn't exist in cities. In rural ridings, the problem of agriculture is one which creates a great deal of work for members.
Mr. Speaker, as far as agriculture is concerned, there are first the farm loans; the member has a lot of work to do to help farmers get those loans. Secondly, there is the crop insurance, which gave a lot of work last year to the members representing rural constituencies, because numerous problems, cropped up in that field, especially in the province of Quebec. Moreover, rural ridings have many other problems that do not exist in urban constituencies. And rural ridings are 20 to 50 times even perhaps 100 times larger than urban constituencies and it costs a lot more to the members who cover them during the year and especially during election time. Even though population is more dense in urban constituencies, there is much more work in rural constituencies than in urban ones.
Mr. Speaker, I must say also that as regards unemployment insurance, and welfare problems, in urban constituencies most of the people usually settle their own problems with the unemployment insurance officers or with welfare bureau, while in rural constituencies, people live far from the centres, they are not accustomed to travel in order to settle their problems 25, 50 or 100 miles from their home. Therefore, they turn to the member of Parliament and it is the rural member who has to look after all those problems, so he has a 100 times more problems to settle that urban members.
At the present time, constituencies are established according to the number of electors. We say: in a given constituency, there must be at least 80,000 electors. Therefore, we enlarge rural constituencies by making one out of two or three and then, we multiply urban constituencies, because we divide them according to the number of electors. That creates a lot of problems in rural constituencies and causes the latter to lose much of their influence in relation to urban constituencies.
According to the new electoral map, the province of Quebec will lose two seats in Parliament while, quite the contrary, it should not lose any, and in view of the new division it will become less important with regard to other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I do not see the advantages of subdividing the constituencies in such a manner. Urban constituencies should be divided according to the size of the territory and rural ridings should cover so many square miles.
Rural constituencies are divided according to the number of electors; some constituencies are 200, 300 or 400 miles long while an urban constituency barely stretches three or four blocks. Mr. Speaker, this creates many problems, especially for the members of rural ridings. To my mind, this is somewhat abnormal and should be revised in order to bring some measure of justice to those ridings, because, frankly, in view of the suggested electoral reform

July 5, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension or electoral boundaries readjustment, rural ridings will be treated unfairly as compared with urban ridings.
Mr. Speaker, no difference is made between an urban riding and a rural riding, between what it may cost a rural member to visit and take care his riding and take care of it, as opposed to an urban member. In view of the situation, if the ridings are to be readjusted as recommended, I feel that rural members should get more money than urban members, because they have much more work to do, many more steps to take and much more money to spend in several sectors.
There is a big difference, Mr. Speaker, between an urban member and a rural member. So I think that we should take all the necessary means and time to discuss and develop some strategy to allow rural ridings at least to be treated on the same level as city ridings because frankly, Mr. Speaker, there have been injustices with respect to rural ridings since the last redistribution.
We are quite prepared, Mr. Speaker, to accept some reforms. There are always reforms to be brought in but they must not be for worse. It must be for better. Reforms must be aimed at improving things, producing a better situation for members of Parliament, particularly in the case we are dealing with. Those recent redistributions will create additional problems for members in rural ridings and those problems must be solved by the members themselves.
If all rural members said what they think, what they claim to be fair for city ridings, they would have something to say. I do not know if they will all rise-they will not all be rising-but in any case I am doing my best, and I ask the government to reconsider the situation before accepting those new redistributions, in short, to take the necessary means to make available to rural ridings as many benefits as to city ridings. Let us have a little justice because working in a rural riding and working in a city riding are certainly not the same.
As I said earlier, the rural member must take care of the problems of farmers and workers who are not used to dealing with their unemployment insurance office when the office is located 100 or 150 miles away and they have neither the means nor the time to travel. This is why the socreds requested that a secretary be appointed in each constituency and be paid by the government. This would ensure a certain degree of equity to the rural constituencies. Perhaps this service is not that necessary in urban constituencies but it is quite necessary in rural ridings. Otherwise the constituencies should be subdivided and should be so reduced as to enable the elected members to see their constituents when required.
When a member is representing a riding such as mine- which includes 85 parishes-and that he is sitting in Parliament 10 or 11 months a year, he has no time to see all parishes. The member is then blamed by his constituents for not visiting them, they feel they do not see him often enough; it is almost impossible for a member to represent ridings including 80, 85 or 90 parishes and cities of 7,000 8,000 10,000 or 12,000 people because he has no time. Therefore, further expanding ridings is an injustice to rural

ridings since they have much more problems than urban constituencies.
Therefore, I think that we should delay the passing of this bill in order to have enough time to change it as we should and make it more available to the people and, in due time, we shall have further suggestions to make.

For an answer, Mr. Speaker, I will state that there are more and more citizens in our region, and probably in the Maritimes as well, who would like to see a total redrawing of the electoral map and a representation based not only on the population but also on regional interests. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after five speeches in a row in support of this bill I find it rather unusual that I should be in disagreement with it. Each previous speaker mentioned representation by population and then went on to deny it. Personally I am rather surprised at the speed at which this legislation appears to be moving along. I did not know until quite late this afternoon that it was to be discussed this evening.
I should like to say a few words about the mechanics of the legislation and its journey through this House. As has been indicated so far, I hope that the debate on this bill will be of a non-partisan variety. It should be, because this should not be the type of bill which is good for the Conservatives, bad for the NDP, or good for the government and bad for the Social Credit. This is a bill which, if we are not very careful, will divide the country on other than party lines. It will pit rural dwellers against city dwellers. It will have people casting aspersions at the Maritimes simply because they are in an advantageous position, viewing distribution in the light of the principle of representation by population.
I do not speak tonight particularly as a Conservative or as a member who is in danger of losing his seat, because whether or not this bill passes makes no difference in my particular constituency. I should like to speak tonight as a British Columbia Member of Parliament. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the recommendations are receiving a great deal of criticism. The operation of the commission, particularly in certain provinces, is being criticized, and I can hardly blame the people of those provinces. A person does not have to be a native of Manitoba or Alberta to see that the commission did not do an equitable job of redividing those two provinces into new constituencies. They cut across national transportation lines. They elongated some constituencies beyond all reason.
It is very difficult to see how the final decision was arrived at in respect to Alberta or Manitoba. Some provinces will lose seats if this legislation is carried out as intended. I can understand the hon. members from Newfoundland being quite upset that they are to lose one seat when New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are not. I can understand the alarm of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) at the number of seats for his province dropping from 21 to 12. This is a great drop in the number of seats, but anyone who has driven through Saskatchewan realizes that the country has been denuded of population in the last twenty years. Acres do not vote, people vote, and votes have to be where people are. People are moving more and more into the cities. I realize that a rural constituency requires additional work, and the hon. member from the Social Credit party who spoke made a very good case for it; but I had the impression that the act provided a 20 per cent quotient for rural constituencies.
We in British Columbia were not going to complain. We have waited patiently since 1964 for this act to come into effect. I think we waited patiently and with good grace

July 5, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension and we did not complain about it. Finally the day was to dawn at the next election when we would have equitable representation in the federal parliament. At least, until tonight when this bill was put in front of us.
I am sure that all caucuses, constituencies and provinces which are about to lose members think that there would be partisan advantage in passing this bill. They may be right, but I would not bet anything on that. The act was intended to take the matter out of political hands. It is very clear from reading Hansard for 1964 that the main intention of the parliament of that day was to get the act out of the House of Commons and have redistribution carried out by a non partisan organization. Whether or not the organization ended up being non-partisan, of course, is a question that could be debated at length. In any case, that was the intention. Now we are denying it.
I suppose we can say that British Columbia will get the seats in the next election after the coming one. It reminds me of Lewis Carroll: You can have jam tomorrow or jam yesterday, but you will never get jam today. Or federal seats in this next election.
What makes us think that the next group of 264 members of parliament after the next election will feel any more inclined to carve up or rearrange the seats that they hold? I am sure every member here feels confident that he can be re-elected, because he was elected on October 30. All he wants is that his boundaries be left alone. But this is not the attitude we should be taking. We should be striving for something higher than that and trying to ensure that people are represented equitably in this country.
There are several suggestions which have been put forward as to how we could find our way out of the dilemma in which we find ourselves. Possibly we should increase the number of seats in the House. When one listens to some of the members talking about giving out two seats here and taking away one seat there, one begins to feel that everybody is going to win prizes and that everyone will be happy. This reminds me of the financing of the Olympic Games, if I can bring in another subject with that remark. According to the financing body, nobody can lose. However, the bitter fact remains that we will not increase the number of members of parliament drastically, and that some provinces will be underrepresented.
I would like to give you a few figures to indicate how badly some of the provinces are treated in this regard at present. Under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, B.C. will have 26 seats. This is the number of se&ts to which we have been looking forward for a considerable time. At present we have 23 seats. Taking away these three seats will mean that you will be reducing the number of seats which B.C. is supposed to have by 14 per cent. That is a sizeable percentage.
Ontario is the other province due to lose seats. They too are to lose three seats. Given the fact they now have 88 seats, the loss in the number of their seats works out to just over 3 per cent, whereas B.C., according to one article I have read, is being robbed of 14 per cent of the seats to which we are entitled, and which we had reason to expect we would have in the next election.

One talks about redistribution. If we are to be equitable to the people of B.C. in comparison with the people of Prince Edward Island and follow the principle of "rep by pop" through to the ultimate-which I do not recommend-B.C. would have 78 seats. That is, if we were able to elect members in the way the lucky citizens of P.E.I. are. The maritime provinces are specially protected from any loss of seats by a constitutional provision. The provinces may not have less members of parliament than senators. However, totally lacking is any true comparison with any representation by rights of the people of British Columbia. It now takes 14 B.C. votes to equal 10 votes in Saskatchewan, and it takes 37 B.C. votes to offset 10 votes in P.E.I.
I do not know if there will be a recorded vote on this measure. I have been given to understand that will not. But if there is a recorded vote I would like to ask the House leaders and the whips, not for the first time in this session, to permit a free vote to find out how the members really feel about this matter. This constitutional measure, which gives certain provinces a great advantage over B.C., and Ontario to a lesser degree, seems to be the stumbling block or the rock on which we continually founder in looking for a solution. If I can go on mixing my metaphors, may I say that any member who does as I am doing and attacks the principle of P.E.I. having four seats is attacking the most sacred cow of all sacred cows in the BNA Act.
We cannot be equitable to the people of Canada until we are willing to go back to basic principles, instead of arguing these petty points that are continually being brought up about the difficulties of this constituency or of that constituency. Each constituency has its own peculiar difficulties. It may be the difficulty of having a bilingual or trilingual population. It may be the difficulty which is that of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), whose constituency is as large as the rest of Canada put together. If he were to hold out for representation by acreage, the way some hon. members do, he would have the equal of the rest of the House. We must come to some kind of understanding that we will get back to basic principles over the difficulties of representation in this vast, complex country of ours.
I am opposed to this bill because I thought the act was moving in the right direction when it came out. We thought it was a move in the right direction and it seemed reasonably fair to the provinces of slow growth or negative growth. I felt that we would gain seats, and I suppose it would be only fair to state that the Conservatives expect to gain three additional seats in the province from which I come. But I suggest that this bill should be defeated and that we should let the people speak on the subject. I have yet to hear any group outside of this House say that there is anything wrong with the redistribution act of 1964. I had to come to Ottawa and become a member of this House to find out who it is in Canada who is really against this redistribution act.

subtopic: ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES READJUSTMENT ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to be very brief tonight in talking on Bill C-208 but there are two or three points that I should like to leave with members of the House.
July 5, 1973

At the outset I want to say that I am one of the members from British Columbia. Our province would stand to gain three seats by the new distribution which is taking place, and the province is certainly entitled to that. This bill more or less gives an 18 month hoist to this new redistribution.
There are several aspects of the redistribution problem which I feel have not been met by the electoral boundaries commissions which have been doing the job throughout Canada. What worries me most of all is that every redistribution that has taken place over the last few years has led to larger and larger rural ridings. The reason for this is obvious, Mr. Speaker; Canadians are becoming more urbanized every year. There is a trend to the larger cities, the bigger centres, with the result that more and more representation is coming from these areas. Thus we find that the hinterland of this great country of ours is gradually losing representation.
I should like to give a good example of this, and I think it is an example which indicates that members of this House should sit down and try seriously to find some kind of formula to solve the problem. I am convinced that we cannot go entirely on representation by population; if we do we are going to get into a very serious jam before long.
Consider the Northwest Territories, which comprise one-third of the area of Canada and is represented by one member on the floor of this House. I say that is not enough representation in the House of Commons for one-third of Canada. Up in the north, Mr. Speaker, tremendous developments are going on in gas, oil and minerals, and companies are going there on an ever-increasing scale. That part of the country needs protection. It needs more people in Ottawa to bring to the attention of the government and the Canadian public what is happening in this vast northern territory which is one of the rich areas of Canada. I want to make it crystal clear that there is not a Canadian in Canada who will not benefit from the resource development that is going to take place in the north. It is impossible for one individual adequately to service the many scattered communities in that vast northland.
Consider the other provinces. We have heard the representations from Manitoba and Saskatchewan but the same trend applies to all the provinces in Canada-the rural areas are getting bigger and bigger. They are becoming monster ridings, so large that an individual cannot adequately represent them in the House of Commons. These are the areas where we have our resources, and resource development takes place to the benefit of those who live in the cities. It is from these areas that the resources pour down to the manufacturing centres. We need more policemen, if you like to put it that way, people living in these areas who come to the floor of the House of Commons and report to the Canadian nation as far as resource and other types of development are concerned. I have no hesitation in saying that some type of formula must recognize and protect the role that the rural members who live in these large areas play in bringing their story to the House of Commons and to the Canadian people.
I want to point out one or two other things as well, Mr. Speaker. I represent a semi-rural riding. Frankly I prefer to represent a semi-rural riding even though it is difficult
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension to service. I think it is more interesting than a city area, but maybe I am biased. I have never represented a city riding. The people in every little town in every riding in this country are entitled to representation, to see their member, to hear him, to have him speak to them at meetings and listen to their complaints.
As time goes on it becomes obvious to anyone who knows anything at all about the sharp expansion in the size of rural ridings that gradually this contact is being lost. You cannot get to many little communities the way you should simply because there are not enough hours in the day and transportation facilities are not adequate. Sometimes it takes a day and a half of tough driving to get to some of these areas, and up in the north, of course, the problem of getting to communities by air is even more difficult.
These people cannot get on a bus and go to the immigration office to have their problems solved, or go down to the unemployment insurance office to get their claim fixed up, or go to the appropriate office to get advice on a passport or on citizenship papers. All this is funnelled through the member in the rural riding, and some allowance should be made for such a situation. Naturally, members in such ridings take care of more of these sort of problems than do members in the cities.
As a result of the redistribution which recently took place in British Columbia we gained another three seats, and there is no doubt that we deserve them. But, Mr. Speaker, ridings are getting bigger. The only criticism I have of the boundaries commission in British Columbia is that they did not use effectively enough the criteria laid down when redistribution was set up, that of 25 per cent below and 25 per cent above the median. They should have been a lot tougher when they were setting their population quotas for some of the rural areas, and this is my main criticism of those who sat on the boundaries commission. They tried to establish a fairly even median in most ridings, and as a result some rural ridings increased in size. Certainly there are some extensive differences in the ridings in British Columbia, but rural ridings are getting larger and larger and we know that if we follow the same tactics when the next redistribution comes as we followed in this one there will be another increase in size.
The House of Commons must devise some type of formula to include consideration of communications, acreage, people, the economy of the area, resource development, etc. I do not think we have shown that kind of consideration in the directions given to the boundary commissions in this particular redistribution.
For that reason, I feel that this bill should receive the endorsement of the House, that we should set up a committee immediately to look into these problems, and that we devise a formula that is not going to take away from Saskatchewan, Manitoba and some of the large rural areas the type of representation in this House to which I think they are entitled.
I am afraid I cannot offer such a solution tonight but I do draw this matter to the attention of members of this House. We must sit down in our party caucuses and try to come up with some kind of fair distribution of seats, and constituency size must be a factor. This continual trend towards increasingly large monster ridings has to stop. If

July 5, 1973

not, I am afraid that the resource development of this country will suffer and the representation of many rural ridings will get the worst of it when redistribution lines are finally drawn.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill under study tonight is intended to delay the electoral boundaries readjustment and we agree on that principle. The bill is certainly not representative of the opinion of all members of this House as only one of all those who spoke until now seems to support it.
Although it is obvious that electoral boundaries must be readjusted it would have been good that the government prepare a wide ranging bill covering every aspect of the electoral reform.
Every year the government presents new bills to readjust electoral boundaries, to control electoral expenses or to lower the voting age. All those bills are of some value but we always have to begin studying it again during the next session.
For instance, when a member sees the boundaries of his constituency modified following an electoral readjustment and new parishes in another riding substituted for some of the parishes he has represented for several years and where he calls everyone by name and knows almost all their problems, he must again make himself familiar with the individuals, the families and their problems. Therefore, members of Parliament are always sad-and rightly so-to see well known regions disappear to be put into other members' hands, and be replaced by other ridings, which compels them to start it all over again.
Mr. Speaker, what I consider as most irregular in a member's life-and hon. members seem to be embarrassed to speak about it in this House-is the service that he must give to his constituents. We are at a disadvantage when it comes to services and the bill now before us, like the one which was recently put forward and discussed among the House leaders, did not refer to this situation, which does not seem to bother anyone.
Mr. Speaker, we have already asked for at least one office in each riding to provide services for the people. In view of all the difficulties, all our social legislations, all provincial legislations, all social problems,-problems which the hon. member is not concerned about but must still try to solve-it is hard to believe that a member of Parliament's office is still located in his living room or his basement, and that the federal government has not made an office available to him in order to render proper services to the people, while in a few provinces which have fewer resources than the federal government, ridings have an office open six days a week, where the members of Parliament have one secretary and a telephone service at their disposal, to make telephone calls to the capital of the province. Recently, a credit card has been put at our disposal and we begin to get used to it.
Mr. Speaker, we do not have any service, and the electoral readjustment that is proposed today, just like the one that was proposed a few months ago, does not refer to it. I live in Granby, a city of 40,000 people, yet if I want to settle unemployment insurance problems, I must go to the Sherbrooke office where the files are. My constituents

must travel by car, lose half a day, pay their expenses and the toll dues on the superhighway, and wait to state their case to the officials.
Almost every Monday, I have to go to Sherbrooke, appear before the arbitration board and help solve the unemployment insurance problems of my constituents. I must take part in the proceedings of the arbitration board in Sherbrooke, Longueuil or Montreal.
As for welfare, there is the Saint-Hyacinte office covering part of my constituency, that of Marieville covering another part, that of Magog covering a third one and that of Sherbrooke a fourth. Evidently, the Granby office looks after the needs of the residents of that town.
All this to say that the electoral reform under consideration makes no reference to these needs. It is not merely a question of readjusting the electoral boundaries and stating that the population must be represented according to the number of voters. Every member of Parliament must represent just about the same number of people. I agree with this principle, but there is more to it than just changing the electoral boundaries: we must provide adequate services to the population.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to this, there should also be a Parliamentary reform in this House. Nothing more than a mere reference to it has been made during the various electoral campaigns; it has been said that the member of Parliament should be allowed to spend Mondays in his riding to meet his constituents and call on various offices when they open, to solve problems that his constituents have to face.
On Saturdays and Sundays, offices are closed. If you have a problem involving CMHC, you will realize that their offices are open on Monday, but closed on Friday evenings. If you have a problem concerning welfare, unemployment insurance, income tax, you find out that offices are all closed during the weekend; and then, on the Monday, the House is sitting. And all this without reference to the 50 or 100 problems involving voters in our ridings that we must face every weekend, problems arising out of our present laws and from the fact that the member of Parliament must help people solve the problems that keep cropping up these days.
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), who is now present in the House, seems anxious indeed to delay the electoral boundaries readjustment, but he has not yet described the kind of service that we shall be able to provide in our ridings by having better means at our disposal.
We are asked as members to provide an adequate service. That is why we have been elected. We are paid for that job. However, we have first a time problem, and second the government does not provide us with the required services and each weekend there are more and more problems thrown into our tap. It seems to me that government members should cease once and for all apologizing and saying: "It is because of the Conservative Party if we have no secretaries in our ridings. It is because of some NDP members who do not want to have secretaries in their ridings.
July 5, 1973

All Social Credit members want to serve their constituents as they have always done it. But we need the tools to that end and we want those tools to be available to all members. That is why I say there is no reason why government members should look for excuses and criticize other parties saying that if members have no secretaries in their ridings it is the fault of such and such a party. As far as I am concerned, I believe there is no excuse; when the government wants to increase or decrease taxes, it introduces a specific bill and the House decides. I am convinced that it is an hide-and-seek game in order to blame members of other parties for the Cabinet's inaction.
Mr. Speaker, we certainly support the bill before us tonight which postpones the electoral boundary readjustment already adopted by the House in order to, as the President of the Privy Council stated, be better equipped, to better identify the problem and allow the administrative apparatus of the Chief Electoral Officer to be ready whenever a general election is declared.
The main trouble is that no general legislation on election reform is being introduced which could deal with election expenses and electoral boundaries; all adjustments would be made automatically in live with given standards and criteria. We could also provide for the setting up of local services in the constituencies, while our colleagues in the Quebec National Assembly for instance, who are representing about a third of the voters we are representing here-since a federal constituency covers from two to three provincial ridings-have a secretary and an office paid for by the provincial government. I have nothing against that. I am not rising to criticize whatever the provincial government is providing for provincial members; in this connection, I must say that the secretaries are hired to deal with people who, unfortunately, are making no distinction between provincial and federal problems. When a constituent has a social welfare problem, he calls his federal member perhaps more often than his provincial member. It cannot be blamed for it. The contituents telephone the hon. member they know best, who they feel is better aware of their problems, whom they trust or think better able to solve their problems most easily.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish the President of the Privy Council would cease making pious wishes and introduce at last legislation of a general nature on the electoral reform so that, in future, we may know where we stand in all areas of expenses, redistribution of constituencies and services, and that Canadian constituents may obtain the services to which they are entitled.
Moreover, it is essential for us, as elected members, to know where we are going and to know that our constituencies will not be changed at the discretion of either a majority or a minority government. At the present time, the circumstances are changing. Because this is a minority government, it does not appear so eager to push forward the already proposed electoral reform. Being aware of that, we would not always be at the mercy of government that would want to make electoral reforms because we would have a permanent master legislation that would enable all members to serve their constituents better as they deserve-because the many problems we are facing require solutions, which means efforts, tools and material,
Adjournment Debate
and that is why MPs are paid. That is why the last time the parliamentary indemnity was increased, we voted against it and proposed that services be provided instead. As a matter of fact, the increase is practically wiped out by income tax, since we often have to hire an additional secretary in our riding who could deal these with a great number of problems that we would not have to handle here in Ottawa, because that is where are the people who need our help to solve their problems. But for that, we need tools, and I hope the president of the Privy Council will realize this once and for all.

TRANSPORT-CREW OF MOTOR VESSEL "TRAVETAL"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express some concern with regard to responses to questions arising out of the level to which this government respects its own laws, particularly in

July 5, 1973
Adjournment Debate
connection with crews on foreign registered vessels operating in coastal trade. I do so because these questions are of concern to Canada's shipping industry, its seamen, shipyards, contractors, longshoremen, freight handlers and anyone else associated with the maritime industry.
I am somewhat concerned, as all hon. members should be, about the loss of jobs to Canadian merchant officers, particularly in connection with , the Travetal which is perhaps the focal part of the question I asked earlier. I am concerned about the loss of these jobs because of the lack of any clearly defined policy with respect to seamen engaged in the coastal trade.
Who are these seamen? Who should they be? Why does Canada not have a merchant marine? I am concerned about what will be done to accommodate those who have lost jobs as a result of the departure of the Travetal. Short-run solutions are not good enough: there is need for clear, positive, central policies to ensure, in perpetuity if you will, employment for this sector of our manpower. Shipping can no longer be regarded as a segment of the transportation industry. It is an industry in itself.
The trend which is involved make the questions I have raised more important. Figures from Statistics Canada show that the number of vessels of non-Canadian registry engaged in coastal trade has increased by some 50 per cent in the last year for which statistics are available. It has gone from 31 to 45. This trend will continue. When will it be recognized? References are made to it in the Darling Report. The simple fact is that as this proportion increases it becomes increasingly difficult to terminate arrangements which have been made with Commonwealth nations or other nations whose ships are engaged in our trade, employing foreign crews. Their foothold is strengthened to the detriment of Canadians seeking to work in our coastal trade. I stress that it is a coastal trade; we no longer have an offshore fleet due to the stupidity of a former Liberal government some years ago.
What we are really talking about is this: will the Travetal be back, and, if so, in what condition? What assistance, if any, is the government lending to this company and other companies toward the maintenance of an adequate shipping service around the coast? The response of the province of Nova Scotia can be gathered from the fact that the appropriate minister in that province has told the public through a press release that he is concerned and will follow with interest any efforts made by Trident to secure an alternative ship. But the officials say no Canadian ship is available. It is interesting to note that at Lauzon, Quebec, there are three ships perfectly adequate for the car-carrying trade, though probably not designed for it. The solution lies here in Canada-a Canadian ship under a Canadian flag. There is no need to go offshore to find it.
The ships to which I refer are there because of the inaction of the government, its lack of interest in a Canadian merchant marine. I am mainly interested, though, in the loss of jobs. I am curious to know whether or not any contact has been made with the use of these ships in mind, and whether or not contact has been made

with Trident through departmental channels to help resolve this matter in the best of our interests.
Part of the answer to many of the questions I should like to raise is presently sub judice, because, as the parliamentary secretary and certain ministers have become aware in recent days, there is a case before the courts. I suppose in fairness, too, I should say that the Travetal may well have left Canada because of the revaluation of the German mark. But there is no question in my mind that its departure was brought about by the real and legitimate fears of Canada's merchant seamen, fears born of frustration on seeing their livelihood sold to citizens of Spain, Portugal, Germany, Singapore. And for what apparent gain?
Why do we do this, and what benefit is it to Canada? Residents of the coastal provinces of Canada enjoy the right of representation in the federal government. But this seems to have been disregarded by this government, as evidenced by its lack of concern for the development of a truly Canadian merchant marine. I cannot accept anything less than an admission by this government that it is responsible for our coasting trade and for the manner and direction in which it operates.
The minister has not fulfilled this responsibility. He says that he has, and that he wants the Darling Report implemented. I think the Atlantic provinces have moved in this direction already. They have created a constructive relationship and have simply to solve one or two more little issues. This demonstrates not only the lack of concern at the small number of vessels attached to the merchant marine but, more importantly, is a manifestation of the fact that the government intends to bring about an effective remedy-

speechtext:
I suggest it answers some of the points raised this evening, and I might point out that these points were also answered on June 6. However, I will attempt to repeat some of that information at this time.
While the Travetal, being a British ship, was permitted to engage in the coastal trade of Canada, she was also subject to other sections of the Canada Shipping Act. The one which caused the problem related to certificates of competency held by masters and officers, who under the act had to be Canadians or others accepted by the minister, such as certain individuals holding Commonwealth certificates.
On March 6 of this year the minister exempted the Travetal from the requirement to carry officers holding
July 5, 1973

Canadian certificates for a period of three months, until June 5, 1973, on the condition that the parties responsible for the operation submitted proposals for compliance with the act. This exemption expired on June 5 in the absence of such proposals.
The purpose of the original exemption was to avoid disruption of service between Halifax and St. John's. Both the Premier of Nova Scotia and the representative of the local international longshoremen's union urged this course. The seamen's unions' strong advocates of the Darling Report were opposed, and with the expiry of the exemption the seafarers' international union took action in the courts to prevent its renewal. However, the minister subsequently granted the Travetal a further conditional two months' exemption on the strict agreement that Commonwealth officers would be carried in a probationary capacity beside the German officers, and would take over at the end of the new exemption period.
The regular crew members, such as seamen and engine room personnel, were not affected. There is nothing in the Canada Shipping Act or in its subordinate legislation to prevent the employment of non-Commonwealth crew in the jobs. All went well until July 1 when, at 10.30 p.m., the master told the probationary Canadian crew members to pack and leave the ship unless they wanted to go to Germany. The Travetal then left Halifax with no pilot and with no customs clearance.
We are now faced with finding another ship which can be operated under some new arrangement. I hope this will not take too long, but in the meantime we anticipate that the Travetal's usual cargo, chiefly new cars and general freight, can be handled without too much difficulty on Gulf service ships.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR TESTS PROPOSED BY FRANCE-CANADIAN REPRESENTATIONS- PARTICIPATION IN POSSIBLE ACTION BEFORE INTERNATIONAL COURT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR TESTS PROPOSED BY FRANCE-CANADIAN REPRESENTATIONS- PARTICIPATION IN POSSIBLE ACTION BEFORE INTERNATIONAL COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was rather difficult tonight to prepare my remarks because I was not certain whether the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) would reply, and sometimes the remarks of speakers should be connected to the subject in at least some distant way.
I have had a long interest in what I consider to be the obscenity of nuclear testing, whether it happens to be done on the part of our allies or those countries with which we have no particular relationship. On February 5 I asked three essential things of the Secretary of State for External Affairs since I was concerned about Canada's position in terms of protesting further nuclear testing on the part of the Republic of France, as framed in the concern expressed by the United Nations, Australia and New Zealand.
I asked further about Canada's efforts to support the New Zealand and Australian application before the World Court. I do not know whether Canada did that, but I was pleased that approximately a week ago the World Court
Adjournment Debate
ruled that France was indulging in illegal acts in continuing tests in the South Pacific.
Finally, I was concerned because of a previous test in Muroroa atoll in respect of which a Canadian vessel had been intercepted on the high seas by a French ship of war. There was damage and an alleged ramming.
I am pleased also to note a release by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the effect that the government of Canada would stand behind one of its citizens by making a representation to the government of France in respect of collecting the damages done to the Greenpeace III captained by David McTaggart when it was approached on the high seas and not in French waters. I am pleased that at last Canada is indulging in this kind of action.
The concern I have is not unique. It is the concern of very many people, not just the people of the so-called nuclear nations but many people around the world.
Just today from my own constituency I received a couple of letters. I shall quote parts of them. One says:
Dear Sir:
My first concern in writing to you this morning is to urge you to do everything in your power to influence the Canadian government to make a tangible contribution to the protest to the French atomic bomb tests in the South Pacific.
Our government has been very tardy in doing anything to help the many nations who are now protesting this action by the French, which could adversely affect the health of many generations to come. And there is no real reason for the tests!
Here is another letter from a constituent in a distant part of my riding which states in part:
Re: Atmospheric Nuclear Test
We are most concerned with Canada's slap-on-the wrist attitude toward atomospheric nuclear testing by any nation.
We are also deeply troubled with having gone to the polls to elect a do-nothing government, which has wasted endless days on bilingualism and capital punishment. . .
And the letter continues. These are not my words; they are the words of some of the people I represent, and I read them into the record because they are important to them as well as to many other people in the country.
Today I made the suggestion that Canada might well support the efforts of New Zealand by sending a naval vessel on a symbolic peaceful protest. Aboard the New Zealand naval vessel-and there is another one standing by ready to sail not into French waters but on a symbolic protect against the continued pollution of the high seas by France from its continued testing-was one cabinet minister from New Zealand. I suggest we should support our sister member of the Commonwealth, or sisters if you include Australia as well as New Zealand, by sending a vessel on a similar protest. There was only room for one cabinet minister aboard the New Zealand vessel because it was packed with nuclear radiation testing equipment, but I suggest quite seriously that if a Canadian vessel were despatched to lend some support there are members of this House on both sides who would be prepared to go on such a mission.
This is not a hostile act. It is a peaceful symbolic protect and worthy of support. Certainly I would be among those people who would be willing to go, and I am certain that

July 5, 1973
Adjournment Debate
there are members of the cabinet who would be as courageous as are those in the New Zealand cabinet. I put this forward in all seriousness and I hope the government will consider this particular initiative.
Before I sit down let me say that I think that the kind of attitude that I have to these matters is best summed up by the following statement, made on July 3, by Prime Minister Kirk of New Zealand:
New Zealand is against all forms of nuclear testing, not merely those which create fall-out. It opposes tests not merely because of the risk to health from an increase in radiation levels, but because we believe that they bring with them a greater danger of the outbreak of nuclear war. The continued explosion of nuclear devices in more than one country creates a climate of indifference in which this danger may easily be overlooked. But the development of more and more deadly means of mass destruction cannot contribute to peace, nor relieve tension. It can only bring closer the day when some nation, somewhere, will put these weapons to use.
New Zealand, therefore, favours a more effective treaty which would outlaw all forms of testing, and to which all nuclear powers and potential nuclear powers were party. Until such a treaty is in existence, New Zealand will continue to speak out against all nuclear testing, and to urge the present nuclear powers to bring their tests programs voluntarily to an end.
That is the kind of initiative, the kind of outspoken absence of timidity, the posture, that I would like to see adopted by our government. I think it is about time we acted in this way. I think we have had too much hush-puppy, pussyfooting diplomacy on the part of our Department of External Affairs. I look forward to the minister rising and telling me that I misjudged him, that the government is really concerned, and that it is going to be aggressive in terms of our search for peace.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR TESTS PROPOSED BY FRANCE-CANADIAN REPRESENTATIONS- PARTICIPATION IN POSSIBLE ACTION BEFORE INTERNATIONAL COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must first inform my colleague that I was astonished at his preliminary remark. My colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hopkins) was prepared, as I was, to answer the hon. member.
I must tell the hon. member that we share his apprehensions about the signs that France is soon going to resume nuclear testing in the South Pacific. But all the same I must say that I failed to understand how one could be aggressive and in favour of peace at one and the same time.
I think that the hon. member is well aware that Canada has, on numerous occasions, and at various forums, stated its opposition to nuclear testing. I am referring to the opposition expressed by our Canadian delegations to the United Nations General Assembly, the Geneva Disarmament Conference, and other international conferences concerned with this problem. Indeed, Canada is known for its outstanding role among the countries seeking to bring an end to these tests. At the 27th Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Canada presented a resolution aimed at opening serious negotiations for a total ban of nuclear tests, which the Assembly adopted by a large majority.
Furthermore, the Canadian delegation gave strong support to a resolution presented by Australia and New Zealand, dealing mainly with nuclear tests in the South Pacific: at the critical moment during the debate, the

intervention of our delegation-which remained in close consultation with the co-authors of the resolution from the time the Assembly opened-ensured the adoption of the resolution in its entirety.
The apprehension of the South Pacific countries about French nuclear testing is all the more understandable in that these are atmospheric tests, which therefore produce readioactive fallout that can be a threat to public health and to the environment. In that respect, Canada could also be exposed to a similar danger, but rather for geographical reasons, following the Chinese nuclear tests. With France, it is the only nuclear power to conduct tests in the atmosphere. That is why on several occasions Canada appealed to those two countries and urge them to put an end to their nuclear tests and adhere to the 1963 treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere.
Here are further examples which could enlighten my hon. colleague. On May 14, the House of Commons passed a resolution asking all nuclear powers to end any testing of nuclear devices and urging especially the government of France to cancel all its proposed tests in the Pacific.
On June 22, the House passed another resolution approving the decision of the International Court of Justice and urging the French government to postpone its proposed tests as decided by the Court.
Following the explosion in the atmosphere of a nuclear device by China on June 27, the Canadian ambassador in Peking expressed his deep regret to the government of that country and asked China to stop all nuclear tests.
I could go on for a long while.
As far as Mr. McTaggart is concerned, I want to remind the hon. member that the government of Canada appealed to the French government in the hope of facilitating a reasonable settlement of his claim without violating the well-established international practice with respect to such maritime accidents.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE INCREASE IN EXTERNAL AID PROGRAMS AND SUPPORT FOR UNITED NATIONS- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE INCREASE IN EXTERNAL AID PROGRAMS AND SUPPORT FOR UNITED NATIONS- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 29 following the government's decision to withdraw the Canadian peace force from Viet Nam I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) to indicate specifically how Canada might augment its contribution to world peace and justice. In his reply the minister referred to increased external aid and Canada's continuing support of the United Nations. He did not, unfortunately, make any reference to more equitable trade policies with the third world.
July 5, 1973

Canada enjoys an enviable reputation in the councils of the world, as our distinguished visitor from India, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, observed in this parliament on June 19. But our reputation could become tarnished and our fine words in favour of global justice could be exposed as hypocrisy if they are not soon matched by new initiatives in the international arena.
Canada's renewed contribution to world harmony, I suggest, should not be made primarily in peacekeeping, important as this has been, nor primarily in more external aid, which has been increasing belatedly. Canada's primary contribution at this stage of world affairs should come in hearing and in heeding the insistent voice of the third world nations, a voice which is demanding justice in international trade. Is this not the principal message which Madame Gandhi wished to convey during her recent visit to Canada? In addressing the two Houses of Parliament she said:
We shall continue to look for technological assistance to bridge the gaps in the structure of our basic industries and our knowhow of new technologies. Our efforts could be more effective if the advanced countries adopted more enlightened trade policies. When it comes to trade, many of the strongest nations behave as though they need protection from the weak. A new outlook which will not condemn developing nations to permanent disadvantage is essential.
Later, in Ottawa and elsewhere, she stressed that India is "more interested in trade than aid" and she said, in what I take to be a pointed remark to the Canadian government, parliament and people:
Although all countries say that they would like to contribute to new trade patterns, they still tend to form rich men's clubs.
As one of the most influential and eloquent spokesmen for the third world, Madame Gandhi was reminding all of us that today the name of the game is not aid but trade. Other voices in Asia, Africa and Latin America have been and are telling us the same message. All of them are insisting that the industrialized nations, including Canada, give preferential treatment to third world countries in international trade. In short, preferential trade policies are more imperative than foreign aid programs if there are to be major reversals in the widening gap that persists between the rich and the poor countries in the world today.
Current world events indicate that we may be on the verge of a whole new international trade and monetary system. President Nixon and Secretary Brezhnev certainly recognized these realities in their trade talks in Washington.
On the international calendar for the seventies there are several crucial negotiating events, such as the GATT, the IMF and various commodity agreements, that are bound to establish world trade and monetary patterns, for years to come. The third world insists on having an equitable voice in these negotiations.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Canada is on record as supporting this very important demand in trade negotiations. The question before us, however, is whether the present government is prepared to act on its commitment by taking the lead among the industrialized nations in supporting third world countries in their bid for trade preferences in these negotiations.
Adjournment Debate
Third world countries have repeatedly requested that a portion of Canadian markets be reserved for imports of goods from the less favoured developed nations. Could the present government not establish marketing mechanisms that would reserve a more substantial portion of our markets for products from third world countries? The Wheat Board, for example, has long existed to assist domestic producers. Could not the same type of assistance be accorded to producers from the less developed countries? The third world countries have also repeatedly requested that Canada guarantee the payment of fair, stable and remunerative prices for such primary products as sugar, coffee, cocoa, etc. The less developed countries continue to suffer severe setbacks from price fluctuations and deteriorating terms of trade. In the forthcoming international commodity negotiations on sugar and coffee, is the present government prepared to support commodity agreements guaranteeing minimum prices that are truly adequate to the needs of the producers?
Of course, the introduction of such measures as market sharing programs and better prices for tropical products would affect our domestic economy. It is, therefore, imperative that changes in Canadian trade policy be paralleled by the introduction of realistic programs for adjustment assistance to aid workers who may have to transfer to other forms of employment. Is the present government prepared to expand the scope of present adjustment assistance programs to aid workers in industries that might have to transfer to other forms of employment? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Canada can best contribute now to the cause of world justice and peace by developing an alternative trade policy which respects the marketing interests of the third world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE INCREASE IN EXTERNAL AID PROGRAMS AND SUPPORT FOR UNITED NATIONS- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would undoubtedly be difficult for me to answer my hon. colleague in three minutes, on a topic as vast as that of aid to developing countries.
I would first like to remind my hon. colleague that our country's total allocations in this sector increased from $338,700,000 in 1969-70, to almost half a million dollars in 1972-73. According to the criteria of the OECD's development assistance committee, the terms and conditions of our development assistance are, and I quote a document published by the government:
-among the most "favourable" offered by the members of this group. Our support for the United Nations development program has also increased. In 1972-73, we spent 25 per cent of our aid funds through multilateral agencies, in accordance with the recommendations contained in the study of our foreign policy.
The matter of Canada's trade relations with underdevelopped countries has several facets. It is complicated, on the one hand, by the various levels of development attained by those countries and, on the other hand, by the vulnerability of the Canadian economy especially of certain disadvantaged areas of Canada in sectors such as those of the textile and footwear industries, for instance, where the underdevelopped countries' exports are more than competitive-
The House of Commons recently passed legislation designed to set up a general preferential tariff for the third world. At the present time, over 70 per cent of those countries exports enter Canada duty-free. Half of the other 30 per cent will receive

July 5, 1973
Adjournment Debate
preferential treatment under the terms of the general preferential tariff.
Canada continues to participate in the agreements on primary products the purpose of which is, in part, to stabilize the price of products of particular importance to the underdeveloped countries. Two meetings will be held this year-
-I refer to the International Agreement on cocoa which was passed last year and which Canada was the first to endorse as an importing country.
I refer also to other fields in which we also lead the way. Finally, I must recall that Canada's role in a good number of those general questions is somewhat unobtrusive.
I keep on quoting:
-Our ability to influence future events is sometimes limited. Moreover, the percentage of our trade with under-developed countries is rather small. On the other hand, should Canada try to change in a unilateral way the trade patterns of the international community as a whole, it could jeopardize her trade relations with a number of her more important trading partners.
Having said that, I thank the hon. member very much for his interest in this question'. The government has already stated that the assistance to international development will be one of the most constructive ways of participating in the international community during the next decade.
